title: Database Systems
description: Database systems: SQL and NoSQL, data modelling, ORMs, search and specialised stores, and caching layers.
objectives: Model data with normalisation and justify the trade-offs
Diagnose a slow query with EXPLAIN and fix it with indexes
Design a cache layer with an invalidation strategy you can reason about

practice.title: Scenario 1 — Every request times out at exactly 30 seconds; the database looks idle
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: The distinguishing clue
Cause
Guardrail
Interviewer probe
symptoms: From 09:14 UTC, p99 latency goes to 30,000ms and then the API returns 504 for most requests. The error is exactly the client's 30s timeout, never a 500. Grafana shows users DB CPU at 6%, active connections 4 of 200. Support says "it started after the 09:05 deploy".
fix: Roll back the deploy. Then kill the leaked sessions and lower the leak window so it self-heals:
Every acquire in a finally, or a withClient-style helper so the pattern cannot be written wrong.
connectionTimeoutMillis: 3_000 so exhaustion is a fast error, not a hang.
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s' so a leak self-destructs.
leak-detection-threshold = 60_000 (Hikari) so the leak names the stack trace at minute one, not in postmortem.

practice.title: Scenario 2 — A SELECT on a 40M-row table suddenly goes from 30ms to 12s, with no code change
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause
The lesson to state
Guardrail
symptoms: The nightly finance report query (GROUP BY customer_id, month over order_lines) jumps from 30ms to 12.4s at ~02:00 each night and returns to 30ms by 02:05. No deploy. No schema change.
fix: Confirm with SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_vacuum, last_autovacuum, vacuum_count, autovacuum_count FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname='order_lines';

Move the report so it does not run during the vacuum: pin the maintenance window (ALTER TABLE order_lines SET (autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 0) makes it faster; pg_repack in the quiet window fixes the underlying bloat), or move autovacuum to a schedule with vacuum_cost_delay tuned, or run the report off-peak.
Short-term: VACUUM (ANALYZE) order_lines; after the window to rebuild the visibility map.
practice.reference:
```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE)
SELECT customer_id, date_trunc('month', created_at) AS m, sum(line_cents)
FROM order_lines WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '90 days' GROUP BY 1,2;
```

practice.title: Scenario 3 — Users report seeing another user's name and order history
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause
The two design lessons

Cache keys are a security boundary. Tenant and user identity must be *inside* the key by construction, not by convention. A key builder that requires a tenant argument (a typed CacheKey factory that takes {tenantId, userId, resource, id} and cannot be called without them) prevents this class of bug structurally.
public on a personalized response is a leak waiting for a CDN. Default to private; opt into public deliberately, with a review checkpoint.
Guardrail
symptoms: Seventeen support tickets in one hour: "I logged in and saw my colleague's dashboard". Not a stale-data ticket. A *data-leak* ticket. Highest severity.
investigation: Stop the bleeding first: disable the cache layer for the affected endpoint with a flag; do not investigate with users' data exposed.
Reproduce locally. Log the Cache-Control, Vary, and the CDN cache key for the endpoint.
Find the cache key construction. The bug is almost always in the key derivation, not in the eviction.
fix: Roll back the key change.
Purge the affected namespace at every layer: Redis (SCAN + DEL or, better, a versioned namespace bump), the CDN (surrogate-key purge), and the app L1 (restart or broadcast).
Audit the log for the exposure window and follow your incident-response policy. Data that crossed users is a notification/regulatory question in many jurisdictions, not just a bug.

practice.title: Scenario 4 — The nightly batch "succeeds" and reports 0 rows, every night
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause
Alert on max(refreshed_at) age > 3× the refresh interval.
Guardrail
symptoms: The monthly-usage rollup job logs refreshed mv_daily_revenue in 4ms and the dashboard shows zeros. It has been wrong for six weeks; nobody noticed because the dashboard was checked by someone with the read replica, and the refresh was writing to the primary.
fix: Run REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY outside an explicit transaction (autocommit), and check the UNIQUE index exists — without it, CONCURRENTLY fails with could not create unique index.
Record the refresh time yourself. Postgres does not track it, so add it:

practice.title: Scenario 5 — ALTER TABLE... ADD COLUMN takes down production
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause

No lock_timeout. The DDL waited for the long-running report query to finish (or forever), and because an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock request queues *ahead* of subsequent requests for the same lock mode ordering, every subsequent query on that table queued behind it. A lock request that cannot be satisfied blocks every later request for the same lock. That queue is the outage, and the migration was only the trigger.
DEFAULT now() is a volatile expression. On the version in use, that forces a full table rewrite under the lock — so the lock would have been held for the entire rewrite anyway.
Guardrail
symptoms: 14:22: a release job runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN shipped_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(). Within 90 seconds, request p99 goes to 60s and the error rate hits 40%. Cancelling the migration recovers the site.
fix: SELECT pg_cancel_backend(<ddl_pid>); — cancel the head of the queue, not the report; cancelling the report does not help if the DDL already holds the queue.
practice.reference:
```sql
SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, now()-query_start AS dur, left(query,100)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock';
```

```sql
SET lock_timeout = '3s';                 -- every DDL, always
SET statement_timeout = '120s';
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN shipped_at timestamptz;   -- nullable, no default: metadata only
-- backfill in batches; then
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN shipped_at SET DEFAULT now();
```

practice.title: Scenario 6 — Sessions all log users out at once, exactly hourly
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause
Guardrail
symptoms: Every hour, on the hour, a spike of re-logins. Redis evicted_keys is climbing. INFO memory shows used_memory at the instance cap and mem_fragmentation_ratio 1.9.
fix: Raise the headroom: maxmemory = 60-75% of instance RAM so Redis evicts before the kernel does.

Split the instances by data class (6.17.3): sessions on their own with allkeys-lru and a long TTL, cache on allkeys-lru, rate limits and locks on noeviction. Now a cache eviction storm cannot log anyone out, and a rate-limiter memory spike cannot fail cache writes.
Add TTLs to keys that had none (a SCAN for keys with no TTL is the classic leak — a final: marker set of keys added to SCAN and check TTL).
practice.reference:
```bash
redis-cli INFO memory | grep -E 'used_memory|maxmemory|fragmentation'
redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory maxmemory-policy
redis-cli INFO stats | grep evicted_keys
redis-cli --bigkeys                 # find the key holding the memory
redis-cli --memkeys                 # sample for large keys
```

practice.title: Scenario 7 — Read replicas lag 40 minutes, then the primary runs out of disk
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause

A long-running query on the replica. hot_standby_feedback = on means the replica tells the primary "do not vacuum rows I still need". A SELECT running for 6 hours against a 3-day-old snapshot pins xmin on the primary, which blocks vacuum, which grows the WAL. That is the *disk* problem.

The replica is simply slower than the primary under load. A long analytical query saturating its I/O means replay cannot keep up. The gap grows; the replication slot holds the WAL so the data is not lost (good), but disk fills (bad).
Guardrail
symptoms: pg_stat_replication.replay_lag climbs steadily to 40 minutes. pg_stat_replication then shows the replica in catchup state and the primary's pg_wal directory grows to 400 GB. Two alarms: replica lag, and disk at 95%.
fix: Kill the offending query on the replica; set max_standby_streaming_delay = 30s (already set) so it *would* have been cancelled — find out why it was not (probably max_standby_streaming_delay = 0, i.e. "never cancel", which someone set during an incident and never reverted).
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_standby_streaming_delay = 30s and restart the replica; move long reports to a separate logical-replica analytics cluster.
Provision standby storage like the primary's (this is the "slow disk stalls synchronous commits" failure from 6.13.3, in its lag form).
Set max_slot_wal_keep_size (e.g. 10GB) so a hopeless replica cannot fill the primary's disk — it gets terminated and re-synced rather than taking down production.
Free disk now: if you have archived the WAL, you can let the slot go and re-pg_basebackup the replica.

practice.title: Scenario 9 — Latency tripled after adding a trigger "for audit purposes"
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause
Drop the old row trigger after the new one is verified.
Ensure the audit function is SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = pg_catalog, public and that audit_log has no trigger on it.
Guardrail
symptoms: A BEFORE UPDATE trigger was added to orders two weeks ago. Since then, bulk updates (UPDATE orders SET status = ... touching 5M rows in a backfill) take 4× longer, and pg_stat_user_tables.n_tup_upd shows no anomaly.
fix: Switch to a statement-level trigger with transition tables (see 6.8.3):
practice.reference:
```sql
SELECT tgname, pg_get_triggerdef(t.oid) FROM pg_trigger t
WHERE tgrelid = 'orders'::regclass AND NOT tgisinternal;
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname='orders';
-- n_tup_upd = 5,000,000 ; the trigger fired 5,000,000 times
```

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER orders_audit_stmt AFTER UPDATE ON orders
REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS newtab OLD TABLE AS oldtab
FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_orders_bulk();
```

practice.title: Scenario 10 — An index exists, the plan "should" use it, and the query is still slow
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause (three, and they compound)
Or a composite GIN: CREATE EXTENSION btree_gin; CREATE INDEX ON events USING gin (tenant_id, payload jsonb_path_ops); so both are in one bitmap.
Run VACUUM events; if recent inserts are missing (pending list).
Re-measure; only then consider a materialized view for the top-N-per-tenant query, which is the shape a materialized view is genuinely for.
The lesson to say out loud
symptoms: SELECT ... WHERE tenant_id = 42 AND metadata @> '{"plan":"pro"}' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50 takes 800ms. There is a GIN index on metadata and a B-tree on (tenant_id, created_at DESC).
fix: Promote the hot field to a typed generated column and index it:
practice.reference:
```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM events WHERE tenant_id = 42 AND payload @> '{"plan":"pro"}'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50;
```

```
Limit  (cost=...)
  ->  Sort  (actual time=812.034..812.040 rows=50)
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 65kB
        ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on events  (actual time=800.1..812.0 rows=498321)
              Recheck Cond: (payload @> '{"plan":"pro"}'::jsonb)
              Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 1204
              Heap Blocks: exact=9841
              ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_payload_idx  (actual time=12..640)
Filter: (tenant_id = 42)     <-- FILTER, not an index condition
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE events ADD COLUMN plan text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (payload->>'plan') STORED;
CREATE INDEX ON events (tenant_id, plan, created_at DESC);
-- Now: tenant_id = 42 AND plan = 'pro' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50
-- is a single index range scan with no sort.
```

practice.title: Scenario 11 — The rate limiter is rejecting legitimate users at 5% of the limit
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause
The same bug class, second instance
Guardrail
symptoms: A dashboard shows "rate limit exceeded" for normal traffic. Instrumented actual request rate is ~5 req/s against a configured limit of 100/min. The rejection rate is ~4%.
fix: Reject requests with no identity explicitly (401) rather than substituting a sentinel — a missing identity must never become a shared bucket.
Derive identity from the authenticated session at the API layer, after auth, not from a client-supplied header.
Hash the identity so it is not a PII key in Redis, and include the route in the key so different endpoints do not share a bucket.
practice.reference:
```bash
redis-cli --scan --pattern 'rl:*' | head -50      # are all users sharing a key?
redis-cli HGETALL 'rl:{login}:abc123'
redis-cli MONITOR | head -20                        # look at the actual keys being touched
```

practice.title: Scenario 12 — A PITR restore promoted at the wrong moment
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Always recovery_target_action = pause, then check pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() against the expected LSN from monitoring, then SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume(); and promote deliberately. This is the guardrail that converts a silent wrong-point restore into a caught one.
Set recovery_target_timeline = 'latest' when recovering along a failover timeline, and be aware it accepts a timeline that an operator created by accident.

If restore_command cannot find a segment in the middle of the range, replay stops and — with promote — you land at the *end* of what was available. That is the same class of failure and the same pause-then-verify guardrail catches it.
Guardrail
symptoms: During a quarterly drill, the restore ran for 40 minutes and then promoted, but the recovered database was 90 seconds *newer* than the intended target. The engineer assumes the target was wrong.
fix: Use recovery_target_lsn or a named restore point instead of a timestamp whenever precision matters:
practice.reference:
```bash
grep recovery_target "$PGDATA/postgresql.auto.conf"
# recovery_target_time = '2024-06-01 14:36:59+00'
# recovery_target_action = promote        <-- the default since PG 12
tail -50 $PGDATA/log/*.log
# LOG:  recovery stopping after WAL location (LSN) "0/2A9F4C50"
# LOG:  selected new timeline ID: 2
# LOG:  database system is ready to accept connections
```

```bash
# Before the incident, record it; or create a point deliberately
psql -c "SELECT pg_create_restore_point('before_incident')"
psql -c "SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn()"          # the LSN to record in monitoring
# At restore time:
recovery_target_lsn = '0/2A9F4C48'
recovery_target_inclusive = off                # stop BEFORE that record
recovery_target_action = pause                 # verify before promoting
```

questions.answer: A parse tree, not data; it is re-planned and expanded on every reference

questions.text: What is a security_barrier view for?
questions.answer: Preventing predicate reordering below user-supplied functions, so security quals are not bypassed

questions.text: Does a view reduce round trips?
questions.answer: No; an ORM querying per view row is an N+1 in disguise
A UNIQUE index, and it cannot run inside a transaction block

questions.text: Does Postgres track a matview's last refresh time?
questions.answer: No — record it yourself and alert on its age

questions.text: What lock does a plain REFRESH take?
questions.answer: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the matview

questions.text: Trigger that fires once per statement with set access?
questions.answer: FOR EACH STATEMENT with REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS newtab

questions.text: What does a BEFORE ROW trigger returning NULL do?
questions.answer: Silently skips the row

questions.text: When do AFTER trigger blocks fire?
questions.answer: At end of statement
Unpinned search_path allows object shadowing; use SET search_path = pg_catalog, public
Only if you declare AFTER TRUNCATE; they are statement-level
Alphabetical by trigger name — name them 01_, 02_

questions.text: Why are row triggers slow on bulk updates?
questions.answer: Per-row interpreter overhead plus per-statement planning; also they block HOT updates

questions.text: What is a deferred constraint trigger for?
questions.answer: Cross-row invariants checked at commit rather than per row
Yes; a function cannot
It cannot run inside your ORM transaction, and partial failure leaves partial state
Constant folding, inlining, and use in expression indexes

questions.text: A STABLE function that reads now()?
questions.answer: One evaluation reused for the whole query — a silent wrong answer
Rolls back to a savepoint; the whole block's work is undone

questions.text: Postgres advisory lock that cannot leak?
questions.answer: pg_advisory_xact_lock — releases at commit/rollback
Concurrency = throughput × hold-time, plus buffer for bursts and maintenance

questions.text: Why is a big pool slower?
questions.answer: Lock contention on shared buffers and relations; throughput plateaus then falls
The proxy's default_pool_size per (db, user) pool
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, plus connectionTimeoutMillis in the pool
Pool waiters climbing while the database is idle; idle in transaction rows with an old state_change
session, transaction, statement

questions.answer: transaction
SET outside a transaction, session advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY, session PREPARE

server_lifetime plus server_check_query/server_check_delay, or a DNS-aware proxy

questions.answer: 60–75%, so Redis evicts before the kernel OOM-kills
json stores exact text; jsonb is parsed, deduped, order-normalized, and indexable
Much smaller index; only @> and @?, no key-exists

questions.text: Making a JSONB field fast to filter?
questions.answer: A STORED generated column (payload->>'x') plus a B-tree index
New entries sit in a small list until autovacuum merges them; recent rows can be invisible to search
websearch_to_tsquery or plainto_tsquery — never to_tsquery on raw input
A (title) > B (body) > C > D
rank/(rank+1), making scores comparable across queries
READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ (with gap locks)
No — each DDL implicitly commits
INSERT IGNORE swallows truncation and other errors, not just duplicates
RETURNING (no MySQL equivalent), plus arrays, ranges, and EXCLUDE
LAST_INSERT_ID(), which is connection-scoped and therefore pool-hostile
GET_LOCK is session-only, has no transaction variant, and leaks through a pool
Commits block indefinitely unless you allow zero standbys (ANY 0 (...)) or set synchronous_commit = local
One RTT per commit, and standby disk speed becomes a write-latency dependency
Wait until the standby applies it; zero loss, but the replica may be promoted mid-transaction
pg_wal_lsn_diff(sent_lsn, replay_lsn) plus pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()
A long replica query blocks primary vacuum, causing bloat
Consensus lease with a majority, plus real fencing (STONITH / storage detach)

questions.text: Why is replication not a backup?
questions.answer: A committed DROP TABLE replicates in milliseconds
Bounding PITR granularity during low-write periods
recovery_target_action = pause, verify the LSN, then resume — otherwise a missed target silently promotes at the archive's end
Sequences are behind the data; the first insert hits a duplicate key — setval from max(id)
The partition key in a WHERE clause the planner can constant-fold; date_trunc(col) = x prunes nothing

questions.text: Unique constraint on a range-partitioned table?
questions.answer: It must include the partition key
DROP is a metadata operation; DELETE is a data operation (WAL, bloat, no disk shrink)
SET lock_timeout = '3s' — a blocked ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request blocks every later request for that lock

questions.answer: CHECK (c IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID → backfill → VALIDATE CONSTRAINT → SET NOT NULL → drop the check

questions.text: When would you *not* use a relational database?
questions.answer: When the dominant workload is a bounded set of key or prefix lookups over a very wide keyspace at extreme ingest, when the read unit and write unit are the same deeply nested document, or when the data is a time-series with per-series retention. Even then, first check whether Postgres with JSONB, partitioning, or an extension covers it — one engine is usually the right answer and every additional engine is an operational cost

questions.text: What is the single biggest mistake in NoSQL adoption?
questions.answer: Migrating because the data is "unstructured" without enumerating the access patterns. NoSQL stores trade query flexibility for write and read performance on *known* queries; an un-enumerated access pattern becomes an ALLOW FILTERING, a Scan, or an N+1

Partition tolerance is not a choice for a distributed system; during a partition you choose between availability and per-operation consistency, and C is scoped to an operation, not a database. The practical axis is latency versus consistency (PACELC)

questions.text: What is linearizable consistency and what does it cost?
questions.answer: A total order where a read after a completed write sees it or something later. Costs: a round trip to a leader or a quorum, and roughly double the read cost in DynamoDB. It is unavailable on GSIs and cannot be used inside a MongoDB transaction

Sequential = all nodes apply writes in one order but reads may be stale. Causal = reads that have seen A also see B (MongoDB causal sessions, Cassandra session timestamps). Read-your-writes is the weakest and the most commonly needed: the writer never sees stale data

questions.text: What is a failure detector, and why is a fixed timeout insufficient?
questions.answer: Failure cannot be observed directly, only inferred from silence. A fixed timeout either causes false evictions (availability blips) or slow detection (longer outage). Phi accrual detectors track a distribution of heartbeat intervals and adapt to GC pauses and jitter

questions.text: Why does a distributed lock need a fencing token?
questions.answer: Because a failure detector can be wrong: a paused process can resume after its lease expired and act on stale authority. A monotonically increasing token checked by the resource makes an old holder's write rejectable. Redlock has this weakness, which is why the Redis project recommends a single instance with SET NX PX plus a token for efficiency locks, and a consensus system plus fencing for correctness locks

questions.text: When are Postgres advisory locks better than a Redis lock?
questions.answer: Whenever you already run Postgres: the lock is transactional, auto-released on commit/rollback (with the xact variant) or on connection close, and it cannot be leaked by a crashed process. Use pg_try_advisory_lock or pg_advisory_xact_lock. Careful with session-level locks on pooled connections

questions.text: How do you prevent a cache stampede?
questions.answer: Single-flight in-process, a distributed lock with a token, or early recompute inside the stale window. Best in practice: stale-while-revalidate so no reader blocks after the first fill, plus TTL jitter so keys do not expire together

Cache-aside keeps the store authoritative and the cache disposable, at the cost of a possible miss on read and an invalidation obligation. Write-through has no staleness window but introduces a dual write that can fail or diverge, and makes the cache non-disposable

questions.text: When is a cache entry a correctness problem rather than a performance one?
questions.answer: When a read can authorize an action (permissions, entitlements, pricing, fraud signals, feature gating for a paid feature), or when a stale value is irreversible (an emailed invoice, a shipped label). Then you need event-driven invalidation or versioned keys, not a TTL
Fixed TTLs loaded together expire together, producing a periodic miss cliff. Jitter of ±20% spreads expiry and lowers peak miss rate substantially for a one-line change

questions.text: What is maxmemory eviction and why is it scary?
questions.answer: When Redis hits its memory cap it starts deleting keys per the policy, which is silent data loss for anything not rebuildable. Keep caches on allkeys-lru and authoritative data on noeviction, on separate instances, so one class cannot evict the other

questions.text: Fixed window vs sliding window vs token bucket?
questions.answer: Fixed: cheapest, 2x burst at boundaries. Sliding log: exact, memory proportional to the limit. Sliding counter: near-exact, two counters. Token bucket: continuous refill, allows a defined burst. Leaky bucket: smooths the *output* rate for a fragile downstream

questions.text: Why is a rate limiter a separate Redis instance?
questions.answer: The limiter's keyspace must not be evictable (noeviction) and its growth must not be able to flush the cache. Sharing an instance couples two unrelated failure modes, and an eviction storm in the cache would hand every client a fresh quota

Either a home-region limiter (extra cross-region latency, a hole if the region is down) or a per-region limiter with the limit divided by region count. State which one and the resulting global limit explicitly

A decision per endpoint, made deliberately: fail closed for authentication, payments, and anything that would be abused; fail open for reads, with metrics and alerting. It must be a config flag that is alerted on, because a stuck fail-open flag during an incident is expensive

Embed when the child is bounded, read only with the parent, and updated with it. Reference when it grows unboundedly, is queried or paged independently, or updates at a different rate. The unbounded-growth rule is the shortcut: anything that grows with time or activity must not be embedded

Equality fields, then Sort, then Range. The sort goes before the range because an in-memory sort is an immediate 100MB-limit failure while a wider range scan is merely slower. Put equality first so the index is reusable for any subset of the equalities

questions.text: What is a multikey index limitation?
questions.answer: An index can contain at most one array field, because two arrays would require parallel array entries. Compound indexes with two array fields are rejected

questions.text: Partial vs sparse vs TTL indexes?
questions.answer: Partial: only documents matching an expression, and the query must be a superset of it. Sparse: only documents where the field is absent — note that null counts as present, so partial is the better soft-delete pattern. TTL: deletion after a deadline, by a background thread, therefore approximate

questions.text: How do you retire an index safely?
questions.answer: Mark it hidden: true (still maintained on write, invisible to the planner), watch the metrics, then drop it. Dropping a live index makes queries that depended on it fall back to a collection scan
Blocking sorts and large pipeline stages refuse to exceed 100MB of in-memory working set. Fixes: narrow the query, provide the sort with an index, or set allowDiskUse: true and accept disk I/O

questions.text: When do you need a MongoDB transaction?
questions.answer: When two documents must change atomically and no cheaper boundary exists. Before using one, try to reshape the data so the unit of change is a single document. Transactions require a replica set, are slow, and are bounded by the oplog window

questions.text: What are change streams and what are their limits?
questions.answer: An oplog-backed cursor with resume tokens. At-least-once, no ordering across collections, bounded by the oplog window (a consumer that falls too far behind must resync), invalidated by a collection drop, and not a durable queue

w: 1 can be rolled back by a failover, so an acknowledged write can be lost. w: "majority" survives a primary change. Combined with a proper election timeout, majority is what you want for anything you cannot reconstruct

questions.text: What is a scatter-gather and what does it cost?
questions.answer: A query that omits the shard key fans out to all shards; each returns up to limit rows, mongos performs a blocking merge sort, and latency is the slowest shard. limit: 10 on 20 shards can pull 200 documents and the 100MB sort limit applies

questions.text: What must a DynamoDB shard key satisfy?
questions.answer: Immutable, never missing, always indexed, high cardinality and even distribution, and matching the dominant query. Also: a unique index must be prefixed by the shard key, so a bare unique _id is only unique per shard

One key at 1,000 WCU/1,000 RCU per second caps your table. Fix by moving a time or sequence component into the sort key, write-sharding with a random prefix, DAX for read-heavy skew, or fanning a read across replicated copies

An LSI shares the base table's capacity (no extra write cost, same key schema prefix) and only supports eventually consistent reads. A GSI is a separate structure with its own read and write capacity and its own eventual consistency. Use sparse GSIs so the index only contains the subset that belongs in it

questions.text: ConsistentRead: false and a missing item?
questions.answer: An eventually consistent read immediately after a write can return nothing at all for that key. Retry; do not conclude the write failed. Strongly consistent reads cost 2x and are not allowed on GSIs

attribute_not_exists(pk) for create-if-absent and a version or value comparison for compare-and-swap. This is the only way to prevent a lost update in a store with no transactions across items. ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure: ALL_OLD lets you report the delta

On-demand is roughly 2x per unit but instant and no-throttle; you pay a double rate for sudden spikes beyond twice the trailing peak. Provisioned with auto scaling is cheaper at steady state and can throttle while scaling reacts

questions.text: DynamoDB Streams and the two-copies problem?
questions.answer: The table and the stream are both views of the truth. Consumers must be idempotent, dedupe by event id, and handle the case where the stream lags the table (read the table for the latest state, then apply the event)

questions.text: Why Cassandra needs one table per query?
questions.answer: No joins, no ad-hoc indexes, no cross-partition predicates. Each query shape gets its own table or materialized view, which multiplies storage and write cost and makes schema evolution a real project
It reads the whole partition and filters in memory, so cost is proportional to partition size and unbounded memory is possible. A debugging tool, and a scheduled outage in production

Reads plus writes must exceed the replication factor for the read and write replica sets to overlap, which is what prevents a read missing an acknowledged write. With N=3, W=2, R=2 guarantees it; W=1, R=1 does not

A coordinator stores a hint for a down replica and delivers it on return. After gc_grace (default 10 days) hints and tombstones are dropped, so a long outage requires nodetool repair or a rebuild. Plan node downtime against your TTL, because a node is UNREACHABLE for twice the TTL after a long outage

Very high write ingest, a small known set of queries stated in advance, bounded partition sizes, time-ordered data with retention, multi-DC with local reads. Wrong for ad-hoc work, reporting, cross-entity transactions, or a small dataset

questions.text: When is a graph database genuinely right?
questions.answer: When traversal depth is unbounded and the relationship carries data: fraud rings, blast radius, multi-hop recommendations, org charts. A one- or two-hop join is faster, transactional, and better documented in a relational store

questions.text: How do you model a hyperedge?
questions.answer: As an intermediate node, because a property-graph relationship connects exactly two nodes. The same applies in a relational schema: an association table whose key includes the set members

questions.text: What is a time-series cardinality trap?
questions.answer: Prometheus series count is the product of targets and label value combinations, so one high-cardinality label (user_id, request_id, error_message, a URL with an id) multiplies memory and can OOM the TSDB. High-cardinality values belong in fields, not labels

HNSW: higher recall, higher memory, slow build, tunable with ef_search, best for read-heavy at up to low millions. IVFFlat: fast build, lower recall, needs representative training data, tunable with probes, better for large batch ingests on memory-constrained nodes

questions.text: Why does filtered vector search lose recall?
questions.answer: The ANN index returns the globally nearest neighbours and the filter is applied afterwards, so a selective filter can leave you with almost no results. Fix with hnsw.iterative_scan, over-fetching, per-tenant partitions, or an engine with native pre-filtering

Up to a few million vectors, modest QPS, embeddings that must join transactionally to relational data, and hybrid search with tsvector. Graduate on volume, QPS, pre-filtered recall at high recall, or multi-region replicas

questions.text: N+1 in an ORM: what causes it?
questions.answer: Lazy relations resolved per row: include without a join strategy, populate, or relations in a loop. Detect with query counts in tests, APM spans grouped by statement shape, and pg_stat_statements showing a cheap statement thousands of times per second

DataLoader batching with a request-scoped cache, eager loading as a SQL join, split queries (WHERE id IN (...) then stitch), or raw SQL. A module-level DataLoader leaks data between requests and is the classic version of this bug

questions.text: What is the ORM interactive-transaction pitfall?
questions.answer: The transaction pins one connection, so any reference to the global client inside the callback escapes the transaction and commits partially. Also: Promise.all gives no parallelism there, and the default 5s timeout punishes any network call

Four separate deploys: add (nullable), backfill in batches, switch reads, drop later. Doing them together makes the first deploy slow and destroys the rollback path. On Postgres, use NOT VALID + VALIDATE CONSTRAINT for foreign keys and NOT NULL, and CONCURRENTLY for indexes

ADD COLUMN with a volatile default, ALTER COLUMN TYPE (rewrites), SET NOT NULL (verifying scan, unless a validated check constraint exists), ADD FOREIGN KEY (locks both tables), and a plain CREATE INDEX (blocks writes). lock_timeout plus retry turns a table-wide stall into a bounded failure

The ORM is the compiler for CRUD-shaped queries; raw SQL for window functions, CTEs, LATERAL, DISTINCT ON, locks, and hints. Keep the schema and migrations in the ORM so there is one source of truth, and never concatenate an identifier from user input

questions.text: When is a repository pattern worth it?
questions.answer: When unit tests genuinely benefit from a no-database double, when the domain must stay free of the ORM, or when two backends coexist during a migration. When it is one backend and a thin CRUD surface, it is indirection with a mapping tax

Writes are not searchable until the next refresh (default 1s). ?refresh=wait_for for read-your-write flows, ?refresh=true only in tests. A smaller refresh interval means more segments, more heap, and more merge work

keyword for exact matching, sorting, and aggregation (stored whole, unanalyzed, with an ignore_above that silently stops indexing long values); text for full-text, analyzed, not aggregatable. A multi-field gives you both
Every new field name becomes a cluster-state entry, capped by total_fields.limit. Fix with dynamic: strict, dynamic templates, the flattened type, or a separate index per entity type

object flattens, losing the association between array element fields; nested gives each element its own Lucene document (correct, slower, more index). Use nested only when you must query array elements independently
from + size is capped at 10,000 and materializes skipped hits. Use a PIT plus search_after with a stable, unique sort tuple including _shard_doc

k1 controls term-frequency saturation, b controls document-length normalisation. Defaults (1.2, 0.75) are fine; most relevance problems are analyzer and field-structure problems, not parameter problems
Changing a synonym filter changes the analysis of the whole index, so it is a reindex or a search-time-only synonym_graph set. Test them and expect relevance to shift

"One row per order line per day." If you cannot state the grain in one sentence, aggregations will disagree, and late or restated facts make it worse. Partition the fact table by date and restate only closed periods

ELT won: land raw, transform in the warehouse where compute and storage are cheap, and keep raw for reprocessing. Batch for stable upstreams, micro-batch for near-real-time dashboards, streaming or CDC for low latency

Not achievable end to end. Build at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent sink: stable event ids, dedupe windows, or a merge/upsert on a natural key, plus checkpointing after side effects are durable

Window on event time with a watermark and an allowed lateness, route older events to a late-arrival path, and recompute affected closed windows. Processing-time windows put a 5-minute-late event in the wrong bucket and your totals never reconcile
An aborted multipart upload is billed forever. AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload in the lifecycle configuration is the single most valuable line there. Also: the multipart ETag is not an MD5

questions.text: When is Postgres FTS the right search answer?
questions.answer: A few million documents, exact prefix matching via pg_trgm, and filters — with the transactional benefit of the data being in the same database. Move to Elasticsearch for analyzers, phrase/proximity tuning, faceting at scale, and multilingual relevance

questions.text: Tenancy isolation: what actually stops a leak?
questions.answer: tenant_id NOT NULL everywhere, the tenant as the leading index column, uniqueness scoped per tenant, cache keys prefixed by tenant, and row-level security as the safety net for the forgotten predicate. Application-level filters alone are a discipline problem, not a control

questions.text: How do you make an audit log trustworthy?
questions.answer: Enforce immutability with database privileges (no UPDATE/DELETE for the app role), capture changes with triggers or CDC rather than application code, add a hash chain for tamper evidence, and set a legal-hold exemption in the retention sweeper

Triggers: complete, zero lag, invisible to developers, write amplification. CDC: no trigger, no write amplification, decoupled, but seconds of lag, an oplog retention bound, and a resync path to operate
There is no rename. CopyObject + Delete is a full billed server-side copy and is not atomic, so the pattern is immutable objects plus a mutable pointer in a database, deleted later

questions.text: What is the most common way a "scalable" NoSQL design fails?
questions.answer: The shard key is chosen for write distribution while the dominant read omits it, so 90% of traffic becomes a scatter-gather. Design the shard key from the access patterns, and confirm with EXPLAIN that queries are targeted

practice.title: Scenario 1 — Every request times out at exactly 30 seconds; the database looks idle
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: The distinguishing clue
Cause
Guardrail
Interviewer probe
symptoms: From 09:14 UTC, p99 latency goes to 30,000ms and then the API returns 504 for most requests. The error is exactly the client's 30s timeout, never a 500. Grafana shows users DB CPU at 6%, active connections 4 of 200. Support says "it started after the 09:05 deploy".
fix: Roll back the deploy. Then kill the leaked sessions and lower the leak window so it self-heals:
Every acquire in a finally, or a withClient-style helper so the pattern cannot be written wrong.
connectionTimeoutMillis: 3_000 so exhaustion is a fast error, not a hang.
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s' so a leak self-destructs.
leak-detection-threshold = 60_000 (Hikari) so the leak names the stack trace at minute one, not in postmortem.

practice.title: Scenario 2 — A SELECT on a 40M-row table suddenly goes from 30ms to 12s, with no code change
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause
The lesson to state
Guardrail
symptoms: The nightly finance report query (GROUP BY customer_id, month over order_lines) jumps from 30ms to 12.4s at ~02:00 each night and returns to 30ms by 02:05. No deploy. No schema change.
fix: Confirm with SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_vacuum, last_autovacuum, vacuum_count, autovacuum_count FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname='order_lines';

Move the report so it does not run during the vacuum: pin the maintenance window (ALTER TABLE order_lines SET (autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 0) makes it faster; pg_repack in the quiet window fixes the underlying bloat), or move autovacuum to a schedule with vacuum_cost_delay tuned, or run the report off-peak.
Short-term: VACUUM (ANALYZE) order_lines; after the window to rebuild the visibility map.
practice.reference:
```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE)
SELECT customer_id, date_trunc('month', created_at) AS m, sum(line_cents)
FROM order_lines WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '90 days' GROUP BY 1,2;
```

practice.title: Scenario 3 — Users report seeing another user's name and order history
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause
The two design lessons

Cache keys are a security boundary. Tenant and user identity must be *inside* the key by construction, not by convention. A key builder that requires a tenant argument (a typed CacheKey factory that takes {tenantId, userId, resource, id} and cannot be called without them) prevents this class of bug structurally.
public on a personalized response is a leak waiting for a CDN. Default to private; opt into public deliberately, with a review checkpoint.
Guardrail
symptoms: Seventeen support tickets in one hour: "I logged in and saw my colleague's dashboard". Not a stale-data ticket. A *data-leak* ticket. Highest severity.
investigation: Stop the bleeding first: disable the cache layer for the affected endpoint with a flag; do not investigate with users' data exposed.
Reproduce locally. Log the Cache-Control, Vary, and the CDN cache key for the endpoint.
Find the cache key construction. The bug is almost always in the key derivation, not in the eviction.
fix: Roll back the key change.
Purge the affected namespace at every layer: Redis (SCAN + DEL or, better, a versioned namespace bump), the CDN (surrogate-key purge), and the app L1 (restart or broadcast).
Audit the log for the exposure window and follow your incident-response policy. Data that crossed users is a notification/regulatory question in many jurisdictions, not just a bug.

practice.title: Scenario 4 — The nightly batch "succeeds" and reports 0 rows, every night
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause
Alert on max(refreshed_at) age > 3× the refresh interval.
Guardrail
symptoms: The monthly-usage rollup job logs refreshed mv_daily_revenue in 4ms and the dashboard shows zeros. It has been wrong for six weeks; nobody noticed because the dashboard was checked by someone with the read replica, and the refresh was writing to the primary.
fix: Run REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY outside an explicit transaction (autocommit), and check the UNIQUE index exists — without it, CONCURRENTLY fails with could not create unique index.
Record the refresh time yourself. Postgres does not track it, so add it:

practice.title: Scenario 5 — ALTER TABLE... ADD COLUMN takes down production
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause

No lock_timeout. The DDL waited for the long-running report query to finish (or forever), and because an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock request queues *ahead* of subsequent requests for the same lock mode ordering, every subsequent query on that table queued behind it. A lock request that cannot be satisfied blocks every later request for the same lock. That queue is the outage, and the migration was only the trigger.
DEFAULT now() is a volatile expression. On the version in use, that forces a full table rewrite under the lock — so the lock would have been held for the entire rewrite anyway.
Guardrail
symptoms: 14:22: a release job runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN shipped_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(). Within 90 seconds, request p99 goes to 60s and the error rate hits 40%. Cancelling the migration recovers the site.
fix: SELECT pg_cancel_backend(<ddl_pid>); — cancel the head of the queue, not the report; cancelling the report does not help if the DDL already holds the queue.
practice.reference:
```sql
SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, now()-query_start AS dur, left(query,100)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock';
```

```sql
SET lock_timeout = '3s';                 -- every DDL, always
SET statement_timeout = '120s';
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN shipped_at timestamptz;   -- nullable, no default: metadata only
-- backfill in batches; then
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN shipped_at SET DEFAULT now();
```

practice.title: Scenario 6 — Sessions all log users out at once, exactly hourly
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause
Guardrail
symptoms: Every hour, on the hour, a spike of re-logins. Redis evicted_keys is climbing. INFO memory shows used_memory at the instance cap and mem_fragmentation_ratio 1.9.
fix: Raise the headroom: maxmemory = 60-75% of instance RAM so Redis evicts before the kernel does.

Split the instances by data class (6.17.3): sessions on their own with allkeys-lru and a long TTL, cache on allkeys-lru, rate limits and locks on noeviction. Now a cache eviction storm cannot log anyone out, and a rate-limiter memory spike cannot fail cache writes.
Add TTLs to keys that had none (a SCAN for keys with no TTL is the classic leak — a final: marker set of keys added to SCAN and check TTL).
practice.reference:
```bash
redis-cli INFO memory | grep -E 'used_memory|maxmemory|fragmentation'
redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory maxmemory-policy
redis-cli INFO stats | grep evicted_keys
redis-cli --bigkeys                 # find the key holding the memory
redis-cli --memkeys                 # sample for large keys
```

practice.title: Scenario 7 — Read replicas lag 40 minutes, then the primary runs out of disk
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause

A long-running query on the replica. hot_standby_feedback = on means the replica tells the primary "do not vacuum rows I still need". A SELECT running for 6 hours against a 3-day-old snapshot pins xmin on the primary, which blocks vacuum, which grows the WAL. That is the *disk* problem.

The replica is simply slower than the primary under load. A long analytical query saturating its I/O means replay cannot keep up. The gap grows; the replication slot holds the WAL so the data is not lost (good), but disk fills (bad).
Guardrail
symptoms: pg_stat_replication.replay_lag climbs steadily to 40 minutes. pg_stat_replication then shows the replica in catchup state and the primary's pg_wal directory grows to 400 GB. Two alarms: replica lag, and disk at 95%.
fix: Kill the offending query on the replica; set max_standby_streaming_delay = 30s (already set) so it *would* have been cancelled — find out why it was not (probably max_standby_streaming_delay = 0, i.e. "never cancel", which someone set during an incident and never reverted).
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_standby_streaming_delay = 30s and restart the replica; move long reports to a separate logical-replica analytics cluster.
Provision standby storage like the primary's (this is the "slow disk stalls synchronous commits" failure from 6.13.3, in its lag form).
Set max_slot_wal_keep_size (e.g. 10GB) so a hopeless replica cannot fill the primary's disk — it gets terminated and re-synced rather than taking down production.
Free disk now: if you have archived the WAL, you can let the slot go and re-pg_basebackup the replica.

investigation: Find the isolation level and the two queries involved. The 40001 under SERIALIZABLE means the planner found a dangerous structure — a read-write dependency cycle. The classic shape is:

practice.title: Scenario 9 — Latency tripled after adding a trigger "for audit purposes"
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause
Drop the old row trigger after the new one is verified.
Ensure the audit function is SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = pg_catalog, public and that audit_log has no trigger on it.
Guardrail
symptoms: A BEFORE UPDATE trigger was added to orders two weeks ago. Since then, bulk updates (UPDATE orders SET status = ... touching 5M rows in a backfill) take 4× longer, and pg_stat_user_tables.n_tup_upd shows no anomaly.
fix: Switch to a statement-level trigger with transition tables (see 6.8.3):
practice.reference:
```sql
SELECT tgname, pg_get_triggerdef(t.oid) FROM pg_trigger t
WHERE tgrelid = 'orders'::regclass AND NOT tgisinternal;
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname='orders';
-- n_tup_upd = 5,000,000 ; the trigger fired 5,000,000 times
```

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER orders_audit_stmt AFTER UPDATE ON orders
REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS newtab OLD TABLE AS oldtab
FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_orders_bulk();
```

practice.title: Scenario 10 — An index exists, the plan "should" use it, and the query is still slow
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause (three, and they compound)
Or a composite GIN: CREATE EXTENSION btree_gin; CREATE INDEX ON events USING gin (tenant_id, payload jsonb_path_ops); so both are in one bitmap.
Run VACUUM events; if recent inserts are missing (pending list).
Re-measure; only then consider a materialized view for the top-N-per-tenant query, which is the shape a materialized view is genuinely for.
The lesson to say out loud
symptoms: SELECT ... WHERE tenant_id = 42 AND metadata @> '{"plan":"pro"}' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50 takes 800ms. There is a GIN index on metadata and a B-tree on (tenant_id, created_at DESC).
fix: Promote the hot field to a typed generated column and index it:
practice.reference:
```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM events WHERE tenant_id = 42 AND payload @> '{"plan":"pro"}'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50;
```

```
Limit  (cost=...)
  ->  Sort  (actual time=812.034..812.040 rows=50)
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 65kB
        ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on events  (actual time=800.1..812.0 rows=498321)
              Recheck Cond: (payload @> '{"plan":"pro"}'::jsonb)
              Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 1204
              Heap Blocks: exact=9841
              ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_payload_idx  (actual time=12..640)
Filter: (tenant_id = 42)     <-- FILTER, not an index condition
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE events ADD COLUMN plan text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (payload->>'plan') STORED;
CREATE INDEX ON events (tenant_id, plan, created_at DESC);
-- Now: tenant_id = 42 AND plan = 'pro' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50
-- is a single index range scan with no sort.
```

practice.title: Scenario 11 — The rate limiter is rejecting legitimate users at 5% of the limit
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Cause
The same bug class, second instance
Guardrail
symptoms: A dashboard shows "rate limit exceeded" for normal traffic. Instrumented actual request rate is ~5 req/s against a configured limit of 100/min. The rejection rate is ~4%.
fix: Reject requests with no identity explicitly (401) rather than substituting a sentinel — a missing identity must never become a shared bucket.
Derive identity from the authenticated session at the API layer, after auth, not from a client-supplied header.
Hash the identity so it is not a PII key in Redis, and include the route in the key so different endpoints do not share a bucket.
practice.reference:
```bash
redis-cli --scan --pattern 'rl:*' | head -50      # are all users sharing a key?
redis-cli HGETALL 'rl:{login}:abc123'
redis-cli MONITOR | head -20                        # look at the actual keys being touched
```

practice.title: Scenario 12 — A PITR restore promoted at the wrong moment
practice.afterTopic: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
items: Always recovery_target_action = pause, then check pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() against the expected LSN from monitoring, then SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume(); and promote deliberately. This is the guardrail that converts a silent wrong-point restore into a caught one.
Set recovery_target_timeline = 'latest' when recovering along a failover timeline, and be aware it accepts a timeline that an operator created by accident.

If restore_command cannot find a segment in the middle of the range, replay stops and — with promote — you land at the *end* of what was available. That is the same class of failure and the same pause-then-verify guardrail catches it.
Guardrail
symptoms: During a quarterly drill, the restore ran for 40 minutes and then promoted, but the recovered database was 90 seconds *newer* than the intended target. The engineer assumes the target was wrong.
fix: Use recovery_target_lsn or a named restore point instead of a timestamp whenever precision matters:
practice.reference:
```bash
grep recovery_target "$PGDATA/postgresql.auto.conf"
# recovery_target_time = '2024-06-01 14:36:59+00'
# recovery_target_action = promote        <-- the default since PG 12
tail -50 $PGDATA/log/*.log
# LOG:  recovery stopping after WAL location (LSN) "0/2A9F4C50"
# LOG:  selected new timeline ID: 2
# LOG:  database system is ready to accept connections
```

```bash
# Before the incident, record it; or create a point deliberately
psql -c "SELECT pg_create_restore_point('before_incident')"
psql -c "SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn()"          # the LSN to record in monitoring
# At restore time:
recovery_target_lsn = '0/2A9F4C48'
recovery_target_inclusive = off                # stop BEFORE that record
recovery_target_action = pause                 # verify before promoting
```

questions.text: When would you *not* use a relational database?
questions.answer: When the dominant workload is a bounded set of key or prefix lookups over a very wide keyspace at extreme ingest, when the read unit and write unit are the same deeply nested document, or when the data is a time-series with per-series retention. Even then, first check whether Postgres with JSONB, partitioning, or an extension covers it — one engine is usually the right answer and every additional engine is an operational cost

questions.text: What is the single biggest mistake in NoSQL adoption?
questions.answer: Migrating because the data is "unstructured" without enumerating the access patterns. NoSQL stores trade query flexibility for write and read performance on *known* queries; an un-enumerated access pattern becomes an ALLOW FILTERING, a Scan, or an N+1

Partition tolerance is not a choice for a distributed system; during a partition you choose between availability and per-operation consistency, and C is scoped to an operation, not a database. The practical axis is latency versus consistency (PACELC)

questions.text: What is linearizable consistency and what does it cost?
questions.answer: A total order where a read after a completed write sees it or something later. Costs: a round trip to a leader or a quorum, and roughly double the read cost in DynamoDB. It is unavailable on GSIs and cannot be used inside a MongoDB transaction

Sequential = all nodes apply writes in one order but reads may be stale. Causal = reads that have seen A also see B (MongoDB causal sessions, Cassandra session timestamps). Read-your-writes is the weakest and the most commonly needed: the writer never sees stale data

questions.text: What is a failure detector, and why is a fixed timeout insufficient?
questions.answer: Failure cannot be observed directly, only inferred from silence. A fixed timeout either causes false evictions (availability blips) or slow detection (longer outage). Phi accrual detectors track a distribution of heartbeat intervals and adapt to GC pauses and jitter

questions.text: Why does a distributed lock need a fencing token?
questions.answer: Because a failure detector can be wrong: a paused process can resume after its lease expired and act on stale authority. A monotonically increasing token checked by the resource makes an old holder's write rejectable. Redlock has this weakness, which is why the Redis project recommends a single instance with SET NX PX plus a token for efficiency locks, and a consensus system plus fencing for correctness locks

questions.text: When are Postgres advisory locks better than a Redis lock?
questions.answer: Whenever you already run Postgres: the lock is transactional, auto-released on commit/rollback (with the xact variant) or on connection close, and it cannot be leaked by a crashed process. Use pg_try_advisory_lock or pg_advisory_xact_lock. Careful with session-level locks on pooled connections

questions.text: How do you prevent a cache stampede?
questions.answer: Single-flight in-process, a distributed lock with a token, or early recompute inside the stale window. Best in practice: stale-while-revalidate so no reader blocks after the first fill, plus TTL jitter so keys do not expire together

Cache-aside keeps the store authoritative and the cache disposable, at the cost of a possible miss on read and an invalidation obligation. Write-through has no staleness window but introduces a dual write that can fail or diverge, and makes the cache non-disposable

questions.text: When is a cache entry a correctness problem rather than a performance one?
questions.answer: When a read can authorize an action (permissions, entitlements, pricing, fraud signals, feature gating for a paid feature), or when a stale value is irreversible (an emailed invoice, a shipped label). Then you need event-driven invalidation or versioned keys, not a TTL
Fixed TTLs loaded together expire together, producing a periodic miss cliff. Jitter of ±20% spreads expiry and lowers peak miss rate substantially for a one-line change

questions.text: What is maxmemory eviction and why is it scary?
questions.answer: When Redis hits its memory cap it starts deleting keys per the policy, which is silent data loss for anything not rebuildable. Keep caches on allkeys-lru and authoritative data on noeviction, on separate instances, so one class cannot evict the other

questions.text: Fixed window vs sliding window vs token bucket?
questions.answer: Fixed: cheapest, 2x burst at boundaries. Sliding log: exact, memory proportional to the limit. Sliding counter: near-exact, two counters. Token bucket: continuous refill, allows a defined burst. Leaky bucket: smooths the *output* rate for a fragile downstream

questions.text: Why is a rate limiter a separate Redis instance?
questions.answer: The limiter's keyspace must not be evictable (noeviction) and its growth must not be able to flush the cache. Sharing an instance couples two unrelated failure modes, and an eviction storm in the cache would hand every client a fresh quota

Either a home-region limiter (extra cross-region latency, a hole if the region is down) or a per-region limiter with the limit divided by region count. State which one and the resulting global limit explicitly

A decision per endpoint, made deliberately: fail closed for authentication, payments, and anything that would be abused; fail open for reads, with metrics and alerting. It must be a config flag that is alerted on, because a stuck fail-open flag during an incident is expensive

Embed when the child is bounded, read only with the parent, and updated with it. Reference when it grows unboundedly, is queried or paged independently, or updates at a different rate. The unbounded-growth rule is the shortcut: anything that grows with time or activity must not be embedded

Equality fields, then Sort, then Range. The sort goes before the range because an in-memory sort is an immediate 100MB-limit failure while a wider range scan is merely slower. Put equality first so the index is reusable for any subset of the equalities

questions.text: What is a multikey index limitation?
questions.answer: An index can contain at most one array field, because two arrays would require parallel array entries. Compound indexes with two array fields are rejected

questions.text: Partial vs sparse vs TTL indexes?
questions.answer: Partial: only documents matching an expression, and the query must be a superset of it. Sparse: only documents where the field is absent — note that null counts as present, so partial is the better soft-delete pattern. TTL: deletion after a deadline, by a background thread, therefore approximate

questions.text: How do you retire an index safely?
questions.answer: Mark it hidden: true (still maintained on write, invisible to the planner), watch the metrics, then drop it. Dropping a live index makes queries that depended on it fall back to a collection scan
Blocking sorts and large pipeline stages refuse to exceed 100MB of in-memory working set. Fixes: narrow the query, provide the sort with an index, or set allowDiskUse: true and accept disk I/O

questions.text: When do you need a MongoDB transaction?
questions.answer: When two documents must change atomically and no cheaper boundary exists. Before using one, try to reshape the data so the unit of change is a single document. Transactions require a replica set, are slow, and are bounded by the oplog window

questions.text: What are change streams and what are their limits?
questions.answer: An oplog-backed cursor with resume tokens. At-least-once, no ordering across collections, bounded by the oplog window (a consumer that falls too far behind must resync), invalidated by a collection drop, and not a durable queue

w: 1 can be rolled back by a failover, so an acknowledged write can be lost. w: "majority" survives a primary change. Combined with a proper election timeout, majority is what you want for anything you cannot reconstruct

questions.text: What is a scatter-gather and what does it cost?
questions.answer: A query that omits the shard key fans out to all shards; each returns up to limit rows, mongos performs a blocking merge sort, and latency is the slowest shard. limit: 10 on 20 shards can pull 200 documents and the 100MB sort limit applies

questions.text: What must a DynamoDB shard key satisfy?
questions.answer: Immutable, never missing, always indexed, high cardinality and even distribution, and matching the dominant query. Also: a unique index must be prefixed by the shard key, so a bare unique _id is only unique per shard

One key at 1,000 WCU/1,000 RCU per second caps your table. Fix by moving a time or sequence component into the sort key, write-sharding with a random prefix, DAX for read-heavy skew, or fanning a read across replicated copies

An LSI shares the base table's capacity (no extra write cost, same key schema prefix) and only supports eventually consistent reads. A GSI is a separate structure with its own read and write capacity and its own eventual consistency. Use sparse GSIs so the index only contains the subset that belongs in it

questions.text: ConsistentRead: false and a missing item?
questions.answer: An eventually consistent read immediately after a write can return nothing at all for that key. Retry; do not conclude the write failed. Strongly consistent reads cost 2x and are not allowed on GSIs

attribute_not_exists(pk) for create-if-absent and a version or value comparison for compare-and-swap. This is the only way to prevent a lost update in a store with no transactions across items. ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure: ALL_OLD lets you report the delta

On-demand is roughly 2x per unit but instant and no-throttle; you pay a double rate for sudden spikes beyond twice the trailing peak. Provisioned with auto scaling is cheaper at steady state and can throttle while scaling reacts

questions.text: DynamoDB Streams and the two-copies problem?
questions.answer: The table and the stream are both views of the truth. Consumers must be idempotent, dedupe by event id, and handle the case where the stream lags the table (read the table for the latest state, then apply the event)

questions.text: Why Cassandra needs one table per query?
questions.answer: No joins, no ad-hoc indexes, no cross-partition predicates. Each query shape gets its own table or materialized view, which multiplies storage and write cost and makes schema evolution a real project
It reads the whole partition and filters in memory, so cost is proportional to partition size and unbounded memory is possible. A debugging tool, and a scheduled outage in production

Reads plus writes must exceed the replication factor for the read and write replica sets to overlap, which is what prevents a read missing an acknowledged write. With N=3, W=2, R=2 guarantees it; W=1, R=1 does not

A coordinator stores a hint for a down replica and delivers it on return. After gc_grace (default 10 days) hints and tombstones are dropped, so a long outage requires nodetool repair or a rebuild. Plan node downtime against your TTL, because a node is UNREACHABLE for twice the TTL after a long outage

Very high write ingest, a small known set of queries stated in advance, bounded partition sizes, time-ordered data with retention, multi-DC with local reads. Wrong for ad-hoc work, reporting, cross-entity transactions, or a small dataset

questions.text: When is a graph database genuinely right?
questions.answer: When traversal depth is unbounded and the relationship carries data: fraud rings, blast radius, multi-hop recommendations, org charts. A one- or two-hop join is faster, transactional, and better documented in a relational store

questions.text: How do you model a hyperedge?
questions.answer: As an intermediate node, because a property-graph relationship connects exactly two nodes. The same applies in a relational schema: an association table whose key includes the set members

questions.text: What is a time-series cardinality trap?
questions.answer: Prometheus series count is the product of targets and label value combinations, so one high-cardinality label (user_id, request_id, error_message, a URL with an id) multiplies memory and can OOM the TSDB. High-cardinality values belong in fields, not labels

HNSW: higher recall, higher memory, slow build, tunable with ef_search, best for read-heavy at up to low millions. IVFFlat: fast build, lower recall, needs representative training data, tunable with probes, better for large batch ingests on memory-constrained nodes

questions.text: Why does filtered vector search lose recall?
questions.answer: The ANN index returns the globally nearest neighbours and the filter is applied afterwards, so a selective filter can leave you with almost no results. Fix with hnsw.iterative_scan, over-fetching, per-tenant partitions, or an engine with native pre-filtering

Up to a few million vectors, modest QPS, embeddings that must join transactionally to relational data, and hybrid search with tsvector. Graduate on volume, QPS, pre-filtered recall at high recall, or multi-region replicas

questions.text: N+1 in an ORM: what causes it?
questions.answer: Lazy relations resolved per row: include without a join strategy, populate, or relations in a loop. Detect with query counts in tests, APM spans grouped by statement shape, and pg_stat_statements showing a cheap statement thousands of times per second

DataLoader batching with a request-scoped cache, eager loading as a SQL join, split queries (WHERE id IN (...) then stitch), or raw SQL. A module-level DataLoader leaks data between requests and is the classic version of this bug

questions.text: What is the ORM interactive-transaction pitfall?
questions.answer: The transaction pins one connection, so any reference to the global client inside the callback escapes the transaction and commits partially. Also: Promise.all gives no parallelism there, and the default 5s timeout punishes any network call

Four separate deploys: add (nullable), backfill in batches, switch reads, drop later. Doing them together makes the first deploy slow and destroys the rollback path. On Postgres, use NOT VALID + VALIDATE CONSTRAINT for foreign keys and NOT NULL, and CONCURRENTLY for indexes

ADD COLUMN with a volatile default, ALTER COLUMN TYPE (rewrites), SET NOT NULL (verifying scan, unless a validated check constraint exists), ADD FOREIGN KEY (locks both tables), and a plain CREATE INDEX (blocks writes). lock_timeout plus retry turns a table-wide stall into a bounded failure

The ORM is the compiler for CRUD-shaped queries; raw SQL for window functions, CTEs, LATERAL, DISTINCT ON, locks, and hints. Keep the schema and migrations in the ORM so there is one source of truth, and never concatenate an identifier from user input

questions.text: When is a repository pattern worth it?
questions.answer: When unit tests genuinely benefit from a no-database double, when the domain must stay free of the ORM, or when two backends coexist during a migration. When it is one backend and a thin CRUD surface, it is indirection with a mapping tax

Writes are not searchable until the next refresh (default 1s). ?refresh=wait_for for read-your-write flows, ?refresh=true only in tests. A smaller refresh interval means more segments, more heap, and more merge work

keyword for exact matching, sorting, and aggregation (stored whole, unanalyzed, with an ignore_above that silently stops indexing long values); text for full-text, analyzed, not aggregatable. A multi-field gives you both
Every new field name becomes a cluster-state entry, capped by total_fields.limit. Fix with dynamic: strict, dynamic templates, the flattened type, or a separate index per entity type

object flattens, losing the association between array element fields; nested gives each element its own Lucene document (correct, slower, more index). Use nested only when you must query array elements independently
from + size is capped at 10,000 and materializes skipped hits. Use a PIT plus search_after with a stable, unique sort tuple including _shard_doc

k1 controls term-frequency saturation, b controls document-length normalisation. Defaults (1.2, 0.75) are fine; most relevance problems are analyzer and field-structure problems, not parameter problems
Changing a synonym filter changes the analysis of the whole index, so it is a reindex or a search-time-only synonym_graph set. Test them and expect relevance to shift

"One row per order line per day." If you cannot state the grain in one sentence, aggregations will disagree, and late or restated facts make it worse. Partition the fact table by date and restate only closed periods

ELT won: land raw, transform in the warehouse where compute and storage are cheap, and keep raw for reprocessing. Batch for stable upstreams, micro-batch for near-real-time dashboards, streaming or CDC for low latency

Not achievable end to end. Build at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent sink: stable event ids, dedupe windows, or a merge/upsert on a natural key, plus checkpointing after side effects are durable

Window on event time with a watermark and an allowed lateness, route older events to a late-arrival path, and recompute affected closed windows. Processing-time windows put a 5-minute-late event in the wrong bucket and your totals never reconcile
An aborted multipart upload is billed forever. AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload in the lifecycle configuration is the single most valuable line there. Also: the multipart ETag is not an MD5

questions.text: When is Postgres FTS the right search answer?
questions.answer: A few million documents, exact prefix matching via pg_trgm, and filters — with the transactional benefit of the data being in the same database. Move to Elasticsearch for analyzers, phrase/proximity tuning, faceting at scale, and multilingual relevance

questions.text: Tenancy isolation: what actually stops a leak?
questions.answer: tenant_id NOT NULL everywhere, the tenant as the leading index column, uniqueness scoped per tenant, cache keys prefixed by tenant, and row-level security as the safety net for the forgotten predicate. Application-level filters alone are a discipline problem, not a control

questions.text: How do you make an audit log trustworthy?
questions.answer: Enforce immutability with database privileges (no UPDATE/DELETE for the app role), capture changes with triggers or CDC rather than application code, add a hash chain for tamper evidence, and set a legal-hold exemption in the retention sweeper

Triggers: complete, zero lag, invisible to developers, write amplification. CDC: no trigger, no write amplification, decoupled, but seconds of lag, an oplog retention bound, and a resync path to operate
There is no rename. CopyObject + Delete is a full billed server-side copy and is not atomic, so the pattern is immutable objects plus a mutable pointer in a database, deleted later

questions.text: What is the most common way a "scalable" NoSQL design fails?
questions.answer: The shard key is chosen for write distribution while the dominant read omits it, so 90% of traffic becomes a scatter-gather. Design the shard key from the access patterns, and confirm with EXPLAIN that queries are targeted

MongoDB

topics.title: Schema design
topics.description: The schema is the contract: every type, field, argument, and enum, defined in SDL. It is the most important artifact in a GraphQL system, because clients generate against it and every field is a permission boundary.
keyConcepts: Scalars
Custom scalar (DateTime, Money, JSON, URL): parsed and serialized in one place with a GraphQLScalarType, with validation. Best for primitives that are genuinely scalar (a timestamp, a decimal).

Wrapper input/output types (Money as an object): self-documenting, allows adding formatted or currency without a breaking change, and gives you a place to hang validation. Prefer this for money, because it lets you add fields later and it forces the currency along with the amount.
Never Float for money or identifiers. Float is a double. Money as integer minor units, ids as ID (which is serialized as a string).
ID is opaque to the client: you may return a base64-encoded internal id, and clients must not parse it.
A JSON scalar is convenient and dangerous — it is an untyped hole in the schema with no validation and no documentation. Restrict it.
Nullability is a design decision with a real cost

String! (non-null) means the server *must* have a value, or the whole containing chain nulls out and the error propagates to the nearest nullable parent. A non-null field that throws takes the entire query's data to null for that subtree.
String (nullable) means "no value is a legitimate, expected outcome", and it gives you somewhere for errors to land without destroying the response.

Rule of thumb: non-null for things the system guarantees and can always produce (an id, a computed total); nullable for things that legitimately may not exist (a user's displayName, a resource that may be gone). Then reserve non-null for fields whose computation is guaranteed to succeed, and nullable for fields that hit a boundary (an external service, a permission check, an optional relation).
[String!]! vs [String!] vs [String]! encode three different promises: no list, no nulls in the list, vs an empty list. Choosing deliberately prevents a whole class of client null-handling bugs.

The trap: making everything non-null looks tidier and produces catastrophic failures — one flaky dependency nulls the entire page and the client shows nothing, with no partial data. This is a common and expensive production lesson.
commonMistakes: all-non-null schemas; Float for money; reusing output types as input types; a JSON scalar as an escape hatch; client-parsing error messages instead of using a code; enums for open sets; positional arguments instead of a single input object; forgetting __resolveType for a union or interface.
practiceTasks: design a schema for a bookstore: Book, Author, Review, with search returning a union, money as a wrapper type, dates as a custom scalar, order lookup as a connection, and a placeOrder mutation with a payload and a typed error union. Then write schema-level tests that resolve every field against fixtures, including a case with a missing author and a case with a null displayName, and confirm the failure mode is a field-level error rather than a null data.

interviewQuestions.text: Why is nullability a design decision and not a detail?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a schema where every field is non-null, and one flaky third-party enrichment call now nulls the entire product page for a few percent of requests. Decision: non-null only for values the system guarantees, nullable at every boundary, and treat nullability as part of the API contract that clients code against. Reasoning: non-null is a promise with a large blast radius. When a non-null field's resolver throws — an unexpected null from a database, a serialization failure, a downstream timeout — GraphQL cannot return a partial value, so it propagates the error upward: the field becomes null, and if its parent is also non-null the parent becomes null, all the way up. One failure in one field of one item can therefore reduce the whole data to null, and the client shows an empty screen with no context. Making the field nullable gives the error somewhere to land: the field is null, the error appears in errors with its path, the parent stays intact, and the client renders the rest of the page. That is the difference between a degraded page and a broken page. Nullability also has a design dimension: User.displayName should be nullable because a user genuinely may not have set one, and making it non-null would force the API to invent an empty string, which is a lie the client cannot distinguish from a real name. Trade-offs: nullable means every client has to handle null, which is annoying in TypeScript, and it is easy to under-apply and end up with everything optional and no guarantees. Failure scenario: a team makes Order.customer non-null because in the database it is a required foreign key, and then an order created through a legacy import path has a dangling customer reference, so one order's customer field errors and, because Order is non-null in a list, the entire orders connection becomes null — the customer's whole order history disappears because of one bad row. Alternative: make the field nullable *and* fix the data integrity, so the schema tells the truth about the possibility of absence. And enforce it in tests: a resolver for a non-null field should never return null, which is exactly what a schema-level test that resolves every field against fixtures will tell you."

What is the default frame, and what does "peer" mean?
