topics.title: The differences that bite hardest
topics.description: The differences that bite hardest within Database Systems: Additional Topics 12.
keyConcepts: Other dialects, briefly

SQLite: single-writer, whole-database locking (BEGIN EXCLUSIVE), no ALTER COLUMN, WITHOUT ROWID tables for small integer keys, WAL mode for concurrent readers with one writer, PRAGMA journal_mode, FTS5 as a module, and a hard ceiling of practical concurrency that makes it an embedded/mobile/CLI store, not a server store.

SQL Server: clustered vs nonclustered indexes (clustered is the table), READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT (row versions, reader-writer non-blocking) vs locking, NOLOCK being a bug not a feature, MERGE being dangerous, IDENTITY, and cross-database/server queries via OPENROWSET/OPENQUERY. Snapshot isolation at the database level (ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION) is the setting everyone forgets.

Oracle: NUMBER, VARCHAR2, empty string *is* NULL, NVARCHAR2 for the national character set, PL/SQL packages, no LIMIT (uses ROWNUM/OFFSET), sequence-per-table (identity columns only from 12c), and SYSDATE being transaction-stable while SYSCOMMIT is wall-clock.

interviewQuestions.text: Default isolation
interviewQuestions.answer: Two apps behave differently on the same code. MySQL's snapshot is taken at the *first read*, not at the transaction start statement

interviewQuestions.text: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a non-existent row
interviewQuestions.answer: Optimistic "check then insert" patterns deadlock under MySQL

interviewQuestions.text: MVCC undo
interviewQuestions.answer: Same "long transaction is dangerous" story, different tables to look at

interviewQuestions.text: SELECT without FOR UPDATE
interviewQuestions.answer: Two different "read your own writes" behaviours

interviewQuestions.text: DDL transactional
interviewQuestions.answer: A failed ALTER TABLE leaves the schema half-migrated; no transactional migration on MySQL, so migrations must be idempotent by construction

interviewQuestions.text: ALTER TABLE cost
interviewQuestions.answer: A MySQL migration on a 100M-row table is a multi-hour table copy plus a lock at the end (the COPY algorithm takes LOCK TABLES)

interviewQuestions.text: ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT <volatile>
interviewQuestions.answer: Test on your exact version

interviewQuestions.text: Identity / auto-increment
interviewQuestions.answer: Sequence-vs-table behaviour affects sharding and failover

interviewQuestions.text: UUID type
interviewQuestions.answer: B-tree fragmentation with v4 on both, but no uuidv7() helper

interviewQuestions.text: Case-insensitive identifiers/strings
interviewQuestions.answer: WHERE name = 'Bob' matches 'bob'. Joins are likewise case-insensitive: indexes are used but comparisons cost collation work

interviewQuestions.text: NULL in unique indexes
interviewQuestions.answer: Same

interviewQuestions.text: Upsert
interviewQuestions.answer: INSERT IGNORE swallows *all* errors (data truncation too), not just duplicates; a classic data-corruption footgun

topics.title: The portable-SQL strategy
topics.description: The portable-SQL strategy within Database Systems: Additional Topics 12.
keyConcepts: Pick one dialect for the app and write raw SQL through a thin query layer (sqlc, Kysely, Drizzle, pg + a query builder) so the dialect lives in one place.

Standardize the type mapping in the driver: timestamptz ↔ DATETIME (store UTC), jsonb ↔ JSON, uuid ↔ CHAR(36)/BINARY(16), boolean ↔ TINYINT(1) (or INT if 3-valued logic matters, because TINYINT can hold values other than 0/1 if your code is careless).
Avoid dialect-only syntax in the hot path: no UPDATE ... JOIN, no INSERT IGNORE, no GROUP BY on non-aggregates, no DATE_ADD/INTERVAL in business logic (do date math in the app or use a library).

Abstract the migration tool, not the SQL: Flyway, Liquibase, or a custom runner that emits engine-specific DDL from one declarative schema definition. Never rely on a MySQL migration being transactional.

Test the semantics, not just the results. A test that asserts "returns 3 rows" can pass on both engines while the *concurrency* behaviour is completely different. Add a test that runs two transactions concurrently and asserts the isolation behaviour you depend on.

Know the 6.12.1 blockers that force an engine choice: no arrays, no RETURNING, no range types or exclusion constraints, weaker FTS, no DDL transactions. If your design needs EXCLUDE ... WITH && for booking, that is a Postgres decision.

"Your Postgres migration failed halfway. What happened, and what is different on MySQL?" → Postgres DDL is transactional so it rolled back; on MySQL each DDL is an implicit commit, so the schema is partially migrated and your migration must be idempotent and resumable.
"Why is INSERT IGNORE dangerous?" → It converts *any* error, including data truncation and constraint violations it did not intend, into a warning, so you lose rows silently.
"How do you get the inserted id on MySQL?" → LAST_INSERT_ID(), which is per-connection, so it must be read on the same connection as the insert, which leaks it into the data-access layer.

"Your MySQL deadlock rate is high. Why?" → Gap locks under REPEATABLE READ, and inconsistent index usage in concurrent multi-table updates. Fixes: index every join/filter key, keep transactions short and in a consistent table order, consider READ COMMITTED.

"What breaks if you move a Postgres app to MySQL?" → The dialect list above; the ones that silently corrupt are case-insensitive string comparison, INSERT IGNORE, missing RETURNING, and non-transactional DDL.

topics.title: Streaming replication in Postgres
topics.description: Streaming replication in Postgres within Database Systems: Additional Topics 13.
keyConcepts: Lag measurement, and the right lag metric
Synchronous vs asynchronous, precisely

Async (synchronous_standby_names = ''): commit returns after the primary flushes its WAL locally. Zero added latency. On primary failure you lose everything not yet replicated — measured in milliseconds to seconds under load.

Sync (synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (r1, r2)'): commit returns after *one* of the listed standbys has flushed the WAL to its own disk (remote_flush, the default). Adds one network round trip to the write path. If no standby is connected and you have not set synchronous_commit = local, the primary blocks indefinitely, waiting for a standby. This is a real and deliberate design (Postgres will not acknowledge a write it has not replicated, so no data loss), but it turns a replica failure into a primary outage.

Quorum sync (ANY 2 (r1, r2, r3) or FIRST 2 (...)): requires k of n standbys. ANY is better for latency (any of the set flushes), FIRST gives a designated primary standby. Costs an extra RTT for the k-th ack and reduces write availability.

synchronous_commit = remote_apply: waits until the standby has *applied* the transaction, so a failover loses nothing at all — at the cost of a round trip plus replay latency, and a write can be rolled back on the replica if it is promoted mid-flight (read-only transaction failures).
synchronous_commit = local: never wait for standbys, even if configured. Useful as an emergency override during a replica incident, and dangerous as a permanent setting.

Degradation policy that people actually use: normally async; a synchronous_standby_names that requires *zero* standbys (ANY 0 (...)) so a replica outage does not block writes; accept that RPO is "the last few seconds" and make the backup/PITR story cover it. Or: sync for a *specific* table or write path by setting synchronous_commit = remote_flush per session for the payments service and leaving it local everywhere else. That per-workload choice is the senior answer.
A concrete model answer on HA architecture
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```sql
-- On the primary: WAL settings
ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_level = replica;         -- minimum for streaming; 'logical' for logical decoding
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_wal_senders = 10;
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_replication_slots = 10;
ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_keep_size = '4GB';        -- retain WAL so a replica can catch up
ALTER SYSTEM SET archive_mode = on;            -- required for PITR
ALTER SYSTEM SET archive_command = 'test ! -f /mnt/wal/%f && cp %p /mnt/wal/%f';
ALTER SYSTEM SET synchronous_commit = on;      -- default; per-transaction can be relaxed
ALTER SYSTEM SET synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (replica1, replica2)';  -- PG 10+
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
```

```ini
# postgresql.conf on the replica
primary_conninfo = 'host=pg-primary.internal port=5432 user=replicator application_name=replica1 sslmode=verify-full'
primary_slot_name = 'replica1_slot'      # prevents WAL removal on the primary
hot_standby = on                         # allows reads while recovering
max_standby_streaming_delay = 30s       # how long to keep trying before cancelling a query
wal_receiver_status_interval = 10s
hot_standby_feedback = on                # replica tells the primary its xmin; prevents vacuum removing needed rows
```

```sql
-- Replica: true end-to-end delay in seconds
SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replay_delay;
-- Primary: per-replica detail
SELECT application_name, state, sync_state,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(sent_lsn, replay_lsn) AS bytes_behind,
       write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;
```

topics.title: Read replicas: routing, lag, and consistency
topics.description: Read replicas: routing, lag, and consistency within Database Systems: Additional Topics 13.
keyConcepts: Replica lag and its user-visible consequences

Read-your-writes violation: user updates their profile, is redirected, and sees the old profile. Fix: route that session to the primary for a window, or (better) write through a cache and read from it, or use a "version/token" where the client sends the version it last saw and the read is WHERE version >= token.

Replication lag spikes during large UPDATEs, index builds, VACUUM, checkpoints, or when the standby's disk is slow. A synchronous replica that falls behind stalls the primary's commits: synchronous_commit waits for the standby's flush, so a slow disk on one replica takes down writes on the whole cluster. That is a real, well-documented failure mode and it is why standby disk must be provisioned like the primary's, not like a backup's.

Hot standby conflict: a read on a replica that has been open longer than max_standby_streaming_delay is cancelled (error 40001). Long analytical queries need max_standby_streaming_delay = 0 (never cancel) plus careful read-only handling, or run on a separate logical-replica analytics cluster.

hot_standby_feedback is a two-edged sword: it prevents vacuum on the primary from removing rows a standby query still needs, but a long-running query on the replica therefore blocks vacuum on the primary and can cause bloat and, eventually, wraparound problems. Turn it on for correctness, monitor pg_stat_database age of the oldest xmin, and keep replica queries short.

topics.title: Failover: automatic, manual, and the decision either way
topics.description: Failover: automatic, manual, and the decision either way within Database Systems: Additional Topics 13.
keyConcepts: Automatic failover (Patroni + etcd/consul)
Manual failover
Verify the primary is truly down (pg_isready, host-level check, not just the proxy).
On the candidate standby: pg_ctl promote -w (or SELECT pg_promote(true, 60)).
Confirm SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() is false and that pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() is close to the old primary's pg_current_wal_lsn().
Update the DNS/VIP and the application's connection string (with the TTL already lowered *before* the incident, which is the step everyone forgets).

Fail back deliberately later, after the root cause is fixed: resync the old primary (re-basebackup it, or re-join as a replica), and only then plan a switchover, ideally during a quiet window. Failback without a resync loses every write made on the new primary.
RTO/RTO arithmetic to say out loud
Automatic failover with Patroni: RTO 30 to 60 seconds, dominated by the leader lease.
Managed (RDS Multi-AZ, Cloud SQL HA, AlloyDB, Aurora): RTO 60 to 120 seconds, more opaque, fewer knobs.
Cross-region failover with a DNS change: RTO 3 to 10 minutes, dominated by DNS TTL propagation and human decision time.
A manual pg_ctl promote with no runbook: RTO "unknown, probably 20 minutes".
commonMistakes: Believing replication is a backup. A DROP TABLE in autocommit replicates everywhere in milliseconds. Backups are the answer (6.14).
Not monitoring pg_stat_replication lag with an alert. Silent replica death is discovered during an incident.
Under-provisioned standby disks, so synchronous commit stalls the primary. Synchronous replication makes the standby's disk speed a write-latency dependency of the primary.
Routing reads to a replica immediately after a write, breaking read-your-writes.
synchronous_standby_names requiring one standby with no ANY 0 fallback, so a replica failure takes down writes.
Failing back without a resync, losing data written on the new primary.
DNS TTL of 300 seconds set at deploy time and "lowered before the incident" never actually done.
Testing failover in staging, where the replicas are idle and the WAL is a trickle. Failover behaviour depends on load and on max_connections being reached.

topics.title: Postgres backup types
topics.description: Postgres backup types within Database Systems: Additional Topics 14.
keyConcepts: Verification, which is not optional

topics.title: WAL archiving and PITR
topics.description: WAL archiving and PITR within Database Systems: Additional Topics 14.
keyConcepts: recovery_target_time = '...' — stop just before a timestamp. Timestamps are timezone- and clock-skew-sensitive, which is why recovery_target_lsn (a byte position, unambiguous) or recovery_target_xid (a transaction id) are safer when you know the exact transaction.
recovery_target_name = 'some_restore_point' — the best option, because you *named* the point. Create one deliberately before a risky migration:
recovery_target_inclusive = on — include the transaction at the target. off stops just before it.

The footgun: if the recovery target is never reached (a wrong timestamp, missing WAL segment), the server replays to the end of the archive and then promotes anyway (recovery_target_action = promote is the default in PG 12+). You then have a database at the wrong point and may not notice. Mitigation: set recovery_target_action = 'pause', check pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() against the expected LSN, then pg_wal_replay_resume(); and record the target LSN before the incident (the primary's pg_current_wal_lsn() at failure time, from monitoring, is the anchor).

The second footgun: a missing WAL segment in the middle of the archive. The restore stops with requested WAL segment ... has already been removed or could not find file ... in archive. You must supply it (from a replica's WAL, from a cross-region archive, or from a longer-retained tier) or you restore to a later point than you intended.
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
Full backup at 02:00 ────────────────────────────────────────► failure at 14:37
   (base image)            WAL segments archived continuously  ┊
   archive_command copies each completed segment to object     ┊  replay to
   storage (S3/GCS with versioning + immutability)             ┘  14:36:59
```

```bash
archive_command = 'aws s3 cp %p s3://pg-wal/$HOSTNAME/%f --sse-kms aws:kms=<key> --only-show-errors'
restore_command = 'aws s3 cp s3://pg-wal/$HOSTNAME/%f %p --sse-kms aws:kms=<key> --only-show-errors'
# Retry forever, with a bounded attempt count; a failed archive_command fills the pg_wal
# directory and takes the primary down, so alerting on it is a P1.
```

```bash
# Restore, step by step (this is what goes in the runbook)
# 1. Provision a same-or-newer major version instance with the same extensions.
# 2. Restore the base backup.
pgbackrest --stanza=db --target-time='2024-06-01 14:36:59-00' restore
# 3. Post-restore: recovery.signal + restore_command in postgresql.auto.conf
touch "$PGDATA/recovery.signal"
echo "restore_command = 'aws s3 cp s3://pg-wal/$HOSTNAME/%f %p'" >> "$PGDATA/postgresql.auto.conf"
echo "recovery_target_time = '2024-06-01 14:36:59-00'"    >> "$PGDATA/postgresql.auto.conf"
echo "recovery_target_action = 'promote'"                  >> "$PGDATA/postgresql.auto.conf"
echo "recovery_target_inclusive = on"                      >> "$PGDATA/postgresql.auto.conf"
pg_ctl -D "$PGDATA" start
# 4. WATCH THE LOG. recovery_target_time reached -> server promotes and accepts writes.
#    Confirm: SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();  SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();
```

topics.title: The restore drill
topics.description: The restore drill within Database Systems: Additional Topics 14.
keyConcepts: The drill, in order, timed, with a written result
What people discover, every time
An extension is missing on the restore instance and the restore fails at the end. Fix: bake the extension list into the provisioning script and diff it against pg_extension in the runbook.

Sequences are behind after a PITR restore: rows exist with IDs above last_value. The application then tries to insert and hits a duplicate key. Fix: after restore, SELECT setval(...) from max(id) for every sequence; automate it as a post-restore step. (pgbackrest has --archive-mode and there is no automatic sequence fixup in PG; on PG 15+ consider identity columns with GENERATED BY DEFAULT and be explicit anyway.)
The disk is too small for the restored database plus WAL replay. Fix: size scratch instances at 1.3x the production data size.
The restore_command credentials are for a role that can read the bucket but not the KMS key. Fix: test the credential path separately in the drill.
Object-lock/WORM retention silently prevents the drill from deleting its scratch artifacts. Fix: exempt the drill account or namespace.
Nobody knows the target LSN. Fix: continuous monitoring that records pg_current_wal_lsn() every 10 seconds, so "restore to just before statement X" is a lookup, not an investigation.
"How do you know your backups work?" → Automated nightly restore + invariant checks plus a quarterly timed human drill, with an RTO measured and published.

"Give me the recovery procedure for 'an engineer ran DROP TABLE orders at 14:36:59 and it committed'." → Provision a scratch instance, pgbackrest --target-time='2024-06-01 14:36:59-00' with recovery_target_action=promote, replay WAL from the base backup, verify the table exists with the expected row count and the recorded LSN, then copy just that table (or the row delta) back to production with an explicit reconciliation; the full database is not restored over production because that would lose 14:37's real writes.
"What is archive_timeout for?" → Bounding PITR granularity during low-write periods, so WAL segments are forced out at a fixed cadence rather than waiting to fill.

"Why is a volume snapshot not a backup?" → It is crash-consistent only, only recoverable with the matching WAL, only as good as the snapshot's replication across regions, and it is trivially deleted along with the volume by an attacker or an errant script.
commonMistakes: Believing a successful backup job means a restorable backup.
No recovery_target_action = pause plus verification, so a mis-specified target silently promotes at the wrong point.
archive_command failures not alerting: pg_wal fills, the primary shuts down to avoid data loss, and now you have an outage *and* no fresh backups.
Backups in the same region/account as the primary, with credentials that the application can read.
No cross-region copy and no immutable/object-locked backups.

Restoring only the database and not the *roles, grants, extensions, and settings*: a restored instance where the app cannot log in. Fix: version the roles in IaC (pg_dumpall --globals-only), and keep postgresql.conf in IaC too.

No archive_timeout: if the write volume is low, a partially-filled 16 MB WAL segment may not be archived for a long time, so your PITR resolution in quiet periods is coarse. Set archive_timeout = 300s so a segment is forced out at least every 5 minutes.
Never rehearsing a *partial* restore (one schema) even though that is the most common real request.
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
PREPARE (weekly, 30 min)
  - Pick a target: "restore orders to 2024-06-01 14:36:59 into a scratch instance"
  - Confirm the archive contains every segment between base backup and target
  - Record the expected LSN and row counts from monitoring (the acceptance criteria)

EXECUTE (quarterly, timed with a stopwatch)
  t+00  Provision a scratch instance, same major version, same extensions
  t+05  Restore base backup (pgbackrest restore --target-time=...)
  t+20  Post-restore config, recovery.signal, start, watch the log to promotion
  t+35  Verify: pg_is_in_recovery() = false
        row counts per critical table vs the pre-incident recorded values
        CHECK constraints still valid: SELECT count(*) FROM each table WHERE NOT (constraints hold)
        application smoke test against the restored instance (read-only)
        pg_sequences / sequence values sane for writes (setval if restoring to an older point)
  t+45  Record actual RTO, what broke, what was missing from the runbook

REPORT (30 min)
  - Update the runbook with what you learned; add the missing monitoring
  - Fix the retention policy if the archive was incomplete
```

topics.title: Declarative partitioning in Postgres
topics.description: Declarative partitioning in Postgres within Database Systems: Additional Topics 15.
keyConcepts: Partition strategies
Pruning, and how to prove it
The DEFAULT partition decision
Retention by partition drop is the whole point
Partitioning trade-offs, honestly
When to partition
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```sql
CREATE TABLE events (
  id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
  tenant_id   bigint NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  kind        text   NOT NULL,
  payload     jsonb  NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,
  PRIMARY KEY (created_at, id)                 -- partition key MUST be in every unique key
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

CREATE TABLE events_2024_06 PARTITION OF events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-06-01') TO ('2024-07-01');
CREATE TABLE events_2024_07 PARTITION OF events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-07-01') TO ('2024-08-01');
CREATE TABLE events_default PARTITION OF events DEFAULT;   -- the safety net: see below

-- Attach an existing table (faster than CREATE ... PARTITION OF for big tables)
CREATE TABLE events_2024_08 (LIKE events INCLUDING ALL);
ALTER TABLE events ATTACH PARTITION events_2024_08
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-08-01') TO ('2024-09-01');
```

```sql
-- Subpartitioning: monthly outer, 4 weekly inner
CREATE TABLE events PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
CREATE TABLE events_2024_06 PARTITION OF events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-06-01') TO ('2024-07-01')
  PARTITION BY RANGE (id);
CREATE TABLE events_2024_06_w1 PARTITION OF events_2024_06
  FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 0);   -- hash subpartitions
```

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM events
WHERE created_at >= '2024-06-15' AND created_at < '2024-06-20';
--  Seq Scan on events  (rows=0)
--    ->  Seq Scan on events_2024_06  (actual rows=412)
--          Filter: ...
--    ->  Seq Scan on events_2024_07  (actual rows=0)   <- pruned
-- Only the partitions that can contain matching rows are scanned.
```

```sql
-- Adding a future partition without blocking (PG 11+ has a shorter lock; PG 12+ can be
-- done in a transaction that does not hold ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for long)
BEGIN;
CREATE TABLE events_2024_09 PARTITION OF events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-09-01') TO ('2024-10-01');
COMMIT;
```

```sql
DROP TABLE events_2023_01;                 -- instant, no row-by-row DELETE, no bloat, no vacuum
-- vs
DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at < '2024-01-01';  -- hours, millions of dead tuples,
                                                     -- WAL for every row, vacuum to follow,
                                                     -- and the table does not shrink on disk
```

topics.title: MySQL partitioning
topics.description: MySQL partitioning within Database Systems: Additional Topics 15.
keyConcepts: No DEFAULT partition keyword: use a catch-all VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE) and REORGANIZE PARTITION to split it. REORGANIZE PARTITION pmax INTO (PARTITION p2024_08 VALUES LESS THAN ('2024-09-01'), PARTITION pmax VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE)).
Only one partition can have MAXVALUE/the catch-all, and it must be last.
Partition pruning requires the partition key in the WHERE clause with a constant or a range the optimizer can evaluate; a function of the column (YEAR(created_at) = 2024) defeats it.
No foreign keys on partitioned InnoDB tables (before MySQL 8.0; still restrictive in 8.0).
Only one partitioning scheme per table, but subpartitioning exists: PARTITION BY RANGE COLUMNS (...) SUBPARTITION BY HASH(...) SUBPARTITION BY 4.
ALTER TABLE ... DROP PARTITION requires ALTER TABLE ... DROP PARTITION and, in some MySQL versions, the partition must not be the only one and partitions_in_use (InnoDB) must be off.
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```sql
CREATE TABLE events (
  id BIGINT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
  tenant_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  created_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  payload JSON NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)              -- partition key must be in every unique key
) PARTITION BY RANGE COLUMNS (created_at) (
  PARTITION p2024_06 VALUES LESS THAN ('2024-07-01'),
  PARTITION p2024_07 VALUES LESS THAN ('2024-08-01'),
  PARTITION pmax    VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE)   -- acts like DEFAULT
);
ALTER TABLE events ADD PARTITION (PARTITION p2024_08 VALUES LESS THAN ('2024-09-01'));
ALTER TABLE events DROP PARTITION p2024_06;        -- instant
ALTER TABLE events TRUNCATE PARTITION p2024_07;    -- instant
```

topics.title: Sharding: the decision, the keys, and the mechanics
topics.description: Sharding: the decision, the keys, and the mechanics within Database Systems: Additional Topics 15.
keyConcepts: Shard on the primary access pattern
Consistent hashing vs range sharding
The shard-key rules to recite

The shard key must be present in every query's predicate you expect to be frequent. A missing shard key means a fan-out to all shards (a scatter-gather), whose latency is the max shard and whose load is N× the data.
Distribution must be even. Measure with the real distribution, not uniform: SELECT tenant_id, count(*) ... GROUP BY 1 and look at the top-1% share.
It must be immutable. Changing a shard key value means moving the row.
It must avoid hot spots. Sequential ids hash unevenly only if the hash is bad; but if you shard by id % N, the newest ids all hit one shard at the right edge — hence uuid/random ids or a salt.
It must be compatible with your transaction boundaries. Cross-shard transactions are either avoided or made asynchronous (a saga).
Cross-shard operations and what they cost
"Partition or shard?" → Partition for retention and pruning on one node; shard when you exceed one node's CPU/RAM/I/O. Partition first, because it is reversible and cheap.

"How do you enforce a unique constraint on a range-partitioned table?" → Include the partition key in the unique key, or keep a separate global unique index table, or add a computed hash sub-key to the unique constraint.

"Your partition has 5000 sub-partitions and planning got slow." → Planning cost scales with partition count; consolidate to two levels (range by month, hash by 16) and raise plan_cache_mode / use prepared statements.
commonMistakes: Partitioning by a key the queries never filter on, so pruning never happens and every query got slower.
Forgetting the partition key must be part of every unique constraint, then discovering you cannot enforce global uniqueness of slug.
Letting the DEFAULT/MAXVALUE partition accumulate rows, then hitting a lock when adding the next month.
Using DELETE for retention instead of DROP PARTITION.
Sharding before measuring, and sharding on id when all queries filter by tenant_id.
Assuming a scatter-gather is free. It is N× the load and it will melt the coordinator.
Doing a global transaction across shards with 2PC because "the ORM makes it easy", then discovering a coordinator SPOF and a latency floor of 2 RTTs minimum plus a lock manager.
Re-sharding by dual-writing without a verification step, ending up with silent divergence.

topics.title: The lock matrix: what each DDL actually does in Postgres
topics.description: The lock matrix: what each DDL actually does in Postgres within Database Systems: Additional Topics 16.
keyConcepts: The four canonical recipes
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```sql
-- Lock queue discipline: never let a DDL wait behind long transactions.
SET lock_timeout = '3s';
SET statement_timeout = '30s';
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN shipped_at timestamptz;
-- If it fails: cancel the ALTER rather than queueing every subsequent
-- query behind it. This one line prevents the classic
-- "one ALTER TABLE queued behind a 30-minute report took the site down".
```

```sql
-- (1) Add a NOT NULL column with a default, without a rewrite or a long lock (PG 11+)
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending';
-- metadata-only when the default is not volatile. On PG 10 and earlier this rewrote
-- the table; the safe portable form is:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status text;                        -- nullable, instant
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status SET DEFAULT 'pending';     -- instant
-- backfill in batches (see below), then:
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status SET NOT NULL;              -- scans; use the CHECK trick
```

```sql
-- (2) Add NOT NULL to a huge table with a short lock (the CHECK trick)
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_status_nn
  CHECK (status IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;            -- brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, no scan
-- backfill (batched)
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_status_nn;  -- SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, online
-- Now the fast path:
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status SET NOT NULL;     -- PG 12+ skips the scan
ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT orders_status_nn;      -- the NOT NULL now guarantees it
```

```sql
-- (3) Add a foreign key online
ALTER TABLE order_lines ADD CONSTRAINT order_lines_order_fk
  FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id) NOT VALID;
-- backfill / verify existing rows satisfy it (or fix the orphans)
ALTER TABLE order_lines VALIDATE CONSTRAINT order_lines_order_fk;
-- new and updated rows are checked immediately from now on
```

```sql
-- (4) Backfill without a long transaction, without a lock storm, resumably
-- Batch by primary key, in small chunks, in its own transaction.
DO $$
DECLARE
  last_id bigint := 0;
  n int;
BEGIN
  LOOP
    WITH moved AS (
      UPDATE orders SET shipped_at = created_at, updated_at = now()
      WHERE id > last_id AND id <= last_id + 5000 AND shipped_at IS NULL
      RETURNING id
    )
    SELECT max(id), count(*) INTO last_id, n FROM moved;
    COMMIT;                     -- release locks, let vacuum catch up
    EXIT WHEN n = 0;
    PERFORM pg_sleep(0.05);     -- yield, keep WAL and replication lag sane
  END LOOP;
END $$;
```

topics.title: The compatibility matrix: what old code needs while new code exists
topics.description: The compatibility matrix: what old code needs while new code exists within Database Systems: Additional Topics 16.

```sql
-- Table is becoming `order_items`, but 200 query references still say `order_lines`.
-- 1. Rename the physical table (instant) -- old code is now broken, so instead:
ALTER TABLE order_lines RENAME TO order_lines_legacy;
CREATE VIEW order_lines AS SELECT id, order_id, sku, qty FROM order_items_v2;
-- 2. New code writes to order_items_v2 through an INSTEAD OF trigger or the app.
-- 3. Migrate readers to order_items_v2 one query at a time.
-- 4. DROP VIEW order_lines; DROP TABLE order_lines_legacy;
-- Note: an updatable simple view works for writes too; a JOIN view needs
-- an INSTEAD OF trigger per operation, which is a maintenance cost.
```

topics.title: Index lifecycle: create, verify, retire
topics.description: Index lifecycle: create, verify, retire within Database Systems: Additional Topics 16.
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```sql
-- Create without blocking writes
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_tenant_created
  ON orders (tenant_id, created_at DESC);
-- If it fails (e.g. a duplicate value), you are left with an INVALID index
-- that is maintained but never used. Check and clean up:
SELECT c.relname, i.indisvalid, i.indisready
FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid
WHERE NOT i.indisvalid;

-- Verify the planner actually uses it before you retire the old one
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT ... WHERE tenant_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50;
-- watch pg_stat_user_indexes: idx_scan must be > 0 over a representative window

-- Retire: drop (fast), but only after the old index shows idx_scan = 0
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_old;   -- Postgres supports CONCURRENTLY for DROP INDEX
```

topics.title: Migration safety as a discipline
topics.description: Migration safety as a discipline within Database Systems: Additional Topics 16.
keyConcepts: Tooling and gates
Migrations are code. They live in version control, are reviewed, and are applied by CI (prisma migrate deploy, Flyway, Liquibase, yoyo, or a dbmate-style runner). Nobody runs DDL from a laptop.

Separate "apply" from "verify". Every migration has a post-condition: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE ..., a data invariant (row counts, checksum of a sample), and an assertion that reads and writes still work. Emit these as metrics.

One migration per deploy, forward-only. No down migrations that drop data. The rollback for a bad migration is *code* rollback (deploy the old code), and the schema change is cleaned up in a later forward migration. This is the only rollback model that works with a distributed fleet.

Advisory lock on migrations. Two app instances starting simultaneously must not both run migrations. Postgres: SELECT pg_advisory_lock(hashtext('migrations')); in the runner. Flyway/Liquibase have this built in.

Feature flags. The migration and the feature rollout are independent. ALTER TABLE succeeds; the new code path is behind a flag; the flag ramps 1% → 10% → 100% with error-rate and latency gates. This is the difference between a migration and an outage.

Canary the schema. For the riskiest changes, apply the migration to one replica/read-replica first, or to a shadow environment restored from a production backup with production-like data volume, and run the query suite against it.
The kill switch and the safety rails
Rollback semantics, stated honestly
A model answer for "how do you do a zero-downtime migration"

"Your ALTER TABLE is queued behind a long-running query and now everything is stuck. What do you do?" → SELECT pg_cancel_backend(pid) / pg_terminate_backend(pid) on the ALTER itself; if the queue is already built, cancelling the head of the queue is the only thing that unblocks the chain; then set lock_timeout so it never happens again, and fix the long query.
"How do you add NOT NULL to a 500M-row table?" → CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID → backfill → VALIDATE CONSTRAINT → SET NOT NULL (fast path) → DROP CONSTRAINT.
commonMistakes: Running DDL without lock_timeout, so a CREATE INDEX or ALTER TABLE queues behind a long report and blocks *every* subsequent query on the table. The queue is the outage.
Adding a NOT NULL column with a volatile default on PG 10 or earlier and discovering it rewrites 800M rows under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.
CREATE INDEX (not CONCURRENTLY) on a hot table during peak traffic.
Renaming a column in one deploy, breaking 200 queries at once.

Deploying code that reads the new column in the same deploy that creates it, then rolling the code back: now the code expects a column that the rolled-back migration would have... (this is fine if migrations are forward-only, but breaks if you also roll back the migration).
Running the migration from a developer's laptop against production.
A backfill in one big transaction, holding locks and bloating the table and blocking vacuum for an hour.
Forgetting that the ORDER BY/index change requires a plan-cache and prepared-statement refresh in some drivers.

topics.title: Why caching is a correctness problem, not a performance trick
topics.description: A cache entry is a *correctness liability* when a stale read can authorize an action, when it is irreversible once acted upon, or when the invalidation path is not guaranteed to run. Performance caching (a rendered product page) is an optimization. Correctness caching (an entitlement check) is a distributed systems problem, because it introduces a second source of truth whose consistency you must now reason about on every write path.
keyConcepts: The three tests for "is this entry a correctness liability?"

Authorization test. Can a stale value let someone do something they should not? (feature flags for paid features, permission checks, entitlement, fraud/risk scores, geo-restrictions, pricing used at checkout, legal consent.)
Irreversibility test. Once the stale value has been used, can you take it back? (an emailed invoice, a shipped label, a charged card, a published post, an exported CSV, a sent SMS.)

Propagation test. Does the write path guarantee the invalidation happens, atomically, and exactly once? (An UPDATE in one service, an UPDATE in a batch job, a direct psql edit, and a rollback all produce different invalidation outcomes.)
Event-driven invalidation (outbox + consumer, or Pub/Sub) *in addition to* a TTL as a safety net.

Versioned keys: the cache key includes a version (e.g. entitlements:{user_id}:{plan_version}), and a write creates a new version rather than overwriting. Old versions expire naturally; readers see either the old or the new value, never a torn one.
Read-through from the authority with a hard invariant: never cache at all; instead, make the read fast (index, replica) and pay the consistency.
Push-on-write (write-through): the write path updates the cache inside the same transaction boundary as best you can, with the known caveat in 6.17.2.
The second-order costs nobody lists

Cache-key cardinality. Every distinct key is memory, and memory is finite. An unbounded cache is a memory leak with a TTL-shaped disguise; it evicts the useful entries (LRU evicts the coldest, which are often exactly the working set you need when the cache is too small).
Cache keys are an API. user:{id}:profile is depended upon by a service, a script, and a dashboard. Renaming it is a migration. Version keys: user:{id}:profile:v2.

A cache turns a "no data" bug into an intermittent bug. Everything that is hard to debug about distributed systems gets *harder* when a cache is in the middle, because the same request returns different answers.

topics.title: Cache-aside, write-through, write-back
topics.description: The three write/read patterns for keeping a cache and a store of record in sync.

topics.title: TTL strategy, eviction policies, and negative caching
topics.description: TTL is the maximum lifetime of an entry. Eviction is the policy by which a memory-constrained store removes entries before the TTL expires. Negative caching is storing the *absence* of a key so that repeated misses do not reach the store.

topics.title: Cache stampede, dog-pile, and thundering herd protection
topics.description: A cache stampede (or dog-pile) is a burst of concurrent requests for the same expired key, each of which misses and each of which issues its own expensive store read. A thundering herd is the same idea at scale: many keys expiring simultaneously, or a cache restart causing every key to miss at once.
keyConcepts: Four defences, in order of how you should actually use them
1. Single-flight (in-process request coalescing)
2. Stale-while-revalidate (SWR)
3. Distributed lock around the recompute
4. Probabilistic early recompute (XFetch)
Thundering herd beyond a single key

Cache restart / flush. Every key misses at once. Mitigation: warm the top-N keys on startup or on a schedule before allowing traffic (readiness gate), or set a large min-cacheable-size and rely on a "serve stale from the previous process" local L1 (which also makes Redis optional for that tier).
Many keys expiring together. Fixed TTL on a whole query result set (e.g. every tenant's dashboard cached at the same time because you warmed them in a loop) → always jitter.
Stampede across regions. Use per-region locking/refresh, not one global lock, otherwise a global lock is itself a single point of failure during a Redis blip.
Monitoring (this is what makes it production-grade)

"A hot key expires and the DB falls over. Walk me through the fix." → Immediate: enable SWR or a refresh lock so no reader blocks; single-flight so only one process recomputes; TTL jitter so it does not recur; add hit-ratio and fill-QPS metrics; then find why one key had 10k req/s (add an L1 local cache or precompute it).
"Why is single-flight not enough?" → It is per process; with N pods you get N misses, and it does nothing for the herd across *different* keys or after a cache restart.
commonMistakes: Single-flight only, with a large fleet and an expensive compute: 50 concurrent DB queries is still a spike.
A refresh lock TTL shorter than the compute time.
DEL without checking the token, so one process releases another's lock.
SWR with no staleUntil ceiling, so a persistently failing compute serves day-old data forever.
Jitter only on the *value* TTL and not on the negative TTL or the lock TTL.
A cache that is a hard dependency with no fail-open path, so a Redis blip is a total outage.
No metric distinguishing "cache miss" from "cache fill for a key that never existed".
Rate-limiting key generation by user-supplied input without a canonicalization step, so ?page=1&page=01 are two keys.

topics.title: Distributed locks: correctness, failure modes, and fencing tokens
topics.description: A distributed lock is a mechanism that ensures at most one of N processes performs a critical section at a time, across process boundaries. It is the most over-used and most frequently *wrongly implemented* piece of infrastructure in backend systems.
keyConcepts: Start with the honest question: do you need one?
A unique constraint in the database is a lock, and a perfect one (it is atomic, transactional, and deadlock-free). "Only one active subscription per user" is a partial unique index, not a Redis lock.
An atomic conditional update is a lock: UPDATE jobs SET status='running', locked_by=$1 WHERE id=$2 AND status='pending' RETURNING id — one of those succeeds and the other gets zero rows.
A serializable transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or advisory locks (6.6, 6.9) is a lock with real guarantees, scoped to the transaction, auto-released on crash.
Idempotency keys remove the need for mutual exclusion in the classic "process the payment exactly once" case.
A queue with SKIP LOCKED is a lock-free work distribution mechanism.

topics.title: Redis data structures: strings, hashes, sets, sorted sets, streams
topics.description: Redis's structures and, more importantly, the *shape* each one implies for memory, atomicity, and the operations you can do in O(1) versus O(log n) versus O(n).
keyConcepts: The rules that keep Redis healthy

KEYS * is banned in production. It is O(N) and blocks the single thread for the duration. Use SCAN (cursor-based, incremental), HSCAN/SSCAN/ZSCAN for members, or maintain an explicit index key (a set of known keys) if you need to enumerate.
SMEMBERS/HGETALL/LRANGE 0 -1 on a large collection blocks the server. Same family of bug.

Big values cost you twice: the keyspace is single-threaded, so a 10 MB value blocks every other client for the transfer time. Keep values small (target under 10 KB; hard ceiling around 1 MB), put bulk in object storage, and store an S3/GCS key in Redis.
UNLINK over DEL for large values: UNLINK frees the memory in a background thread, DEL frees it synchronously.

Transactions (MULTI/EXEC) are not ACID. No rollback, no isolation; commands are executed in order without interleaving from *other* clients. (An EXEC can return per-command errors, and other clients' commands *cannot* interleave inside, which is the actual guarantee.)

Lua scripts give you atomicity. A script runs to completion with no other client interleaving, which is what makes compare-and-delete and check-and-increment correct. Keep them short: a slow script blocks the whole server, and in Redis 7 there is an EVALSHA/FUNCTION distinction plus script effects replication.
SCAN guarantees: returns elements present throughout the full iteration, may return duplicates, may return nothing new. Design for that (idempotent processing).
Memory policy per instance, from 6.17.3.

maxmemory accounting: INFO memory → used_memory, used_memory_rss, mem_fragmentation_ratio (a high ratio means the allocator is fragmented; activedefrag helps), evicted_keys (must be zero on a noeviction instance and near-zero by design on a cache).
When Redis is the wrong tool
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```bash
# Leaderboard: O(log N) per update, O(log N + M) to read the top M
ZADD leaderboard:weekly 1500 "user:1" 1490 "user:2" 1620 "user:3"
ZREVRANGE leaderboard:weekly 0 9 WITHSCORES        # top 10
ZRANGEBYSCORE leaderboard:weekly 1500 +inf          # everyone above 1500
ZRANK leaderboard:weekly "user:2"                  # my rank (O(log N))
ZINCRBY leaderboard:weekly 5 "user:1"              # update my score
ZREMRANGEBYRANK leaderboard:weekly 0 -1001         # trim to top 1000
ZUNIONSTORE leaderboard:global 2 leaderboard:weekly leaderboard:alltime WEIGHTS 2 1

# Delay queue / scheduled work
ZADD schedule 1717200000 "job:42"                  # score = unix timestamp (when)
ZRANGEBYSCORE schedule -inf $(date +%s) LIMIT 0 100 # due now; claim with ZPOPMIN or ZREM
```

```ts
// Pipeline + multi for bulk work: one round trip, still not atomic across clients
const p = redis.pipeline();
for (const id of ids) p.zincrby('article:42:views', 1, String(id));
await p.exec();

// Transaction for a multi-command atomic unit
await redis.multi().set('a', '1').incr('counter').exec();
```

topics.title: Redis persistence: RDB, AOF, and what you lose in each
topics.description: RDB is a point-in-time binary snapshot of the whole dataset, taken on a schedule or on a save trigger. AOF (Append-Only File) is a sequential log of every write command, replayed on startup. Each loses something different.
keyConcepts: What you actually lose in each, stated precisely
RDB: everything since the last snapshot. If you can recompute the data (a cache), that is free. If not, it is a real RPO measured in minutes.

AOF everysec: up to 1 second of writes. On a crash of the Redis *process*, the data on disk is at most 1 second stale. If Redis runs on an instance that disappears (node failure, AZ outage), the last fsync may be older — the durability guarantee is only as good as your disk.

AOF always: nothing, at the cost of a disk fsync per write (0.1 to 5 ms, and catastrophic on network storage). Use it when the RPO is zero *and* the storage is a local NVMe with a battery-backed cache. Then understand that fsync is still lying if the drive lies.
Neither saves you from a bad write. AOF faithfully replays FLUSHALL, SET key <wrong>, and the INCR that overflowed. redis-check-aof will not tell you the value was wrong.

Neither replaces a backup. Redis's persistence protects against a process crash; it does not protect against flushall, a corrupted file, an accidental CONFIG SET dir, or a region loss. Ship periodic RDB/backup copies to object storage.
The fork problem and stop-writes-on-bgsave-error
A concrete durability decision to state in an interview
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```conf
# RDB
save 3600 1        # save if >= 1 key changed in the last hour
save 300 100      # save if >= 100 keys changed in the last 5 min
save 60 10000     # save if >= 10000 keys changed in the last minute
dbfilename dump.rdb
dir /var/lib/redis
rdbcompression yes
rdbchecksum yes
stop-writes-on-bgsave-error yes     # do NOT silently accept writes you cannot snapshot

# AOF
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec        # the pragmatic setting
no-appendfsync-on-rewrite yes
auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100
auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb
aof-use-rdb-preamble yes    # store the base as RDB, append as AOF: faster load
```

```bash
redis-check-rdb dump.rdb          # validate
redis-check-aof --fix appendonly.aof   # validate, and truncate to the last valid command
```

topics.title: Redis Cluster, Sentinel, and replication
topics.description: Replication: a primary and N replicas, each with a full copy. One writer (unless you deliberately allow replica writes, which is a footgun).

topics.title: Redis Pub/Sub and Streams
topics.description: Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget messaging: PUBLISH delivers to currently-connected SUBSCRIBE clients in O(N) and delivers to nobody who was not connected. Streams are an append-only log of entries with consumer groups, acknowledgements, and pending-entry tracking: a durable queue.

topics.title: Rate limiting algorithms: token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window
topics.description: A rate limiter enforces a bound on request rate. The four families differ in *what they bound* and therefore in what shape of traffic they permit.

topics.title: Session storage and the session-store decision
topics.description: A session is server-side state keyed by an opaque identifier in the client. The decision is *where* that state lives: in the application's memory, in a database, in Redis, in a signed cookie, or in a client-side store.
keyConcepts: The properties that decide it, in order

Revocation requirement. Can you log a user out *right now*, everywhere, including from a stolen token? If yes, you need server-side state (or a denylist), so cookies-with-server-state or short-lived JWTs plus a refresh-token denylist.
Horizontal scaling. In-process sessions require sticky sessions, which couples your load balancer to your app deployment and make a node loss a session-loss event for every user on it.
Size and shape. Sessions holding a shopping cart or a wizard's partial state can exceed the 4 KB cookie limit fast. Redis or a DB is required.

Cost. Redis: ~1 KB per session in memory; 100k active sessions ≈ 100 MB. Postgres: a row plus indexes, and every session read is a query you pay for on the hot path (mitigated by pooling; still more expensive than Redis and it adds to your primary's load).
Compliance and audit. If sessions must be auditable or revokable centrally, a database table wins; Redis is not an audit log.

Failure behaviour. Redis down ⇒ session validation fails. Decide: fail closed (503, "please retry") for authenticated pages, or a stateless fallback (accept a signed-but-unverified cookie? never) — the answer is a short-lived "grace token" or accepting the outage. Note that this is one of the strongest arguments for putting *only an identifier* in the cookie and the state in Redis, so the failure is a clean 503 rather than a security hole.
The security rules
Session id: 128 bits of CSPRNG entropy, never sequential, never derived from anything guessable. 32 bytes from crypto.randomBytes.

Cookie flags: HttpOnly (no JS access ⇒ no XSS theft), Secure (TLS only), SameSite=Lax or Strict (CSRF mitigation), Path=/, a narrow Domain (or none), and __Host- prefix (which requires Secure, no Domain, and Path=/) to prevent subdomain cookie-tossing.
Rotate the session id on privilege change (login, password change, MFA completion) to defeat session fixation.
Idle timeout and absolute timeout, both enforced server-side. An absolute timeout of, say, 12 hours means a stolen token cannot be used indefinitely regardless of activity.
commonMistakes: Sequential or low-entropy session ids.
Not setting HttpOnly, so one XSS exfiltrates every session.
Sliding expiry that never actually happens because EXPIRE on every request (write amplification) or, worse, is never called, so sessions expire mid-use.
Sticky sessions as the only scaling plan, with no session store, so a deploy logs out every user.
Sessions in Postgres with no expires_at index, so the cleanup job is a sequential scan on a hot table.
A JWT with a 30-day expiry and no revocation story.
Storing the session id in localStorage (XSS-readable) instead of a cookie.
Trusting X-Forwarded-For from any source when deriving the session's IP binding.

topics.title: HTTP and CDN caching headers
topics.description: HTTP caching is a protocol between client, proxy, and origin, expressed in headers. Private caches (browsers) may store a response for one user; shared caches (CDNs, reverse proxies) store one copy for everyone, which is why a Set-Cookie or a Vary mistake on a shared cache is a data leak.

topics.title: Multi-layer caching coherence: the invalidation problem
topics.description: Coherence is the property that all copies of a piece of data, across all cache layers, agree up to a stated bound. With one cache, "invalidation" is a DEL. With four layers (browser, CDN, reverse proxy, Redis, plus read replicas in the database), invalidation is a distributed, at-least-once, best-effort operation, and the system is correct only because every layer has a bounded TTL.
keyConcepts: The layers, outermost to innermost, and what invalidates each

topics.title: CAP, without the slogan
topics.description: CAP, without the slogan within Database Systems: Additional Topics 18.
keyConcepts: If your system is distributed across a network, partition tolerance is not a choice. Network partitions are not an exotic failure; they are routine (a switch reboot, a NAT timeout, a rolling deploy, a misrouted packet). Every distributed system must keep operating during a partition, so every distributed system is P. What you actually choose is the *behaviour during* a partition.

"C" is per-operation, not per-database. A system can offer linearizable reads on one key, eventual reads on another, and asynchronous replication to the warehouse. Consistency is a property of an operation against a set of replicas, and a good answer quantifies it per endpoint.

"A" is rarely a free choice either. Availability during a partition means two replicas may accept conflicting writes, so you need reconciliation: last-write-wins (with clock skew as a real hazard), vector clocks or hybrid logical clocks, CRDTs, or a quorum that makes divergence bounded rather than impossible.
The practical axis is latency vs consistency, not C vs A. "CAP is a theorem, PACELC is the useful one" is the interview-grade version.
The honest framing to give out loud

topics.title: PACELC
topics.description: PACELC within Database Systems: Additional Topics 18.

topics.title: Consistency models, with concrete examples
topics.description: Consistency models, with concrete examples within Database Systems: Additional Topics 18.
keyConcepts: "Eventual" is meaningless without a bound. Say "eventual with a convergence SLO of under 2 seconds at p99, monitored by the replication-lag metric, with a read-your-writes override for the writer" rather than "eventually consistent".

Consistency is paid per read. Going from an eventually consistent to a strongly consistent read is a capacity and latency purchase (DynamoDB charges twice the RCUs; MongoDB's linearizable read requires a primary and a majority-committed read point). Design so that only the operations that need it pay for it.

topics.title: Failure detectors
topics.description: Failure detectors within Database Systems: Additional Topics 18.
keyConcepts: Failure detector components: a heartbeat period (how often to probe or ack), a timeout (how long to wait before suspecting), and an *accusation* step (broadcast the suspicion so peers agree, otherwise different nodes suspect different nodes and split the cluster).

Phi accrual failure detector (Cassandra, Akka): instead of a binary timeout, track an exponentially weighted distribution of heartbeat arrival intervals and report a *suspicion level* phi. phi > 8 is a common "declare failure" threshold. This adapts to jitter and GC pauses far better than a fixed timeout.

Why a fixed timeout is fragile: a too-short timeout produces false positives, so healthy nodes are ejected and you get an availability blip for nothing; a too-long timeout means slow detection and a longer period of unavailable writes. Cross-reference 6.1–6.17 for how the same tradeoff shows up as innodb_lock_wait_timeout, statement_timeout, and Postgres wal_sender_timeout.

Timeouts must be hierarchical, not uniform. RPC timeout < database query timeout < HTTP request timeout < client timeout, with real slack at each layer. Every incident traced to "the request took 30 seconds" usually began as a per-hop timeout that was too long, so failures piled up instead of shedding load.

Fencing: a detector can be wrong. Any lock or lease must be protected by a monotonically increasing token (see 6.20) so a partitioned, later-recovered process cannot perform a destructive write after it lost the lease.

Acks are not receipts. A client timing out does not mean the write failed; it may have succeeded and the ack was lost. Every mutating RPC needs an idempotency key, otherwise a retry double-charges a card.

topics.title: Latency budgets
topics.description: Latency budgets within Database Systems: Additional Topics 18.
keyConcepts: Method to say out loud

topics.title: Decision table: requirement to store
topics.description: Decision table: requirement to store within Database Systems: Additional Topics 18.
keyConcepts: Decision procedure to recite in an interview
List the top 5 access patterns with their read/write ratio, volume, latency target, and consistency requirement.
Identify the data classes with a hard correctness requirement (money, inventory, permissions) and put them in a transactional engine. Everything else is negotiable.

For the negotiable classes, ask: is the keyspace wide and the query set closed? If yes, a wide-column or key-value shape is cheap. If the shape is nested and you want ad-hoc field queries, a document store.

Ask what you would need to *delete* if you chose wrong, and what the migration path is (dual-write with an outbox, backfill, cutover, drop). "How would you undo this choice" is a senior question and almost nobody asks it.

Sanity-check the operationally boring truth: how many databases will this team run in 18 months, and who gets paged when one is down at 3am? A single Postgres with two or three well-chosen extensions is frequently the highest-scoring answer.
commonMistakes: reciting CAP as a pick-two menu; claiming a system is "eventually consistent" without a convergence target; treating consistency as a database-wide switch; assuming a fixed heartbeat timeout is a failure detector; designing a lease without a fencing token; adding a new datastore without an invalidation or dual-write plan; saying "NoSQL scales horizontally" without naming the key; picking a graph database for a fixed two-hop join; ignoring that the answer must also be operable by the team.
practiceTasks: take a system you know (a music service, a food delivery app) and write a one-page data-class matrix: data class, store, consistency level, latency target, invalidation/derivation strategy, and what breaks first at 100x. Then measure real latencies for a Redis GET, a Postgres point read, and a SELECT of 50 rows locally, and check your table against the numbers; the gap between guess and measurement is the lesson.

interviewQuestions.text: What is the NoSQL taxonomy, and what is each family's data unit and query model?
Why is "pick two of three" a misstatement of CAP?
interviewQuestions.answer: "CAP is a theorem about behaviour *during* a network partition, not a menu. In any system spread over more than one network hop, partitions are a matter of time, so partition tolerance is mandatory and the real choice is what happens when nodes cannot talk. I prefer PACELC because it names the trade-off in the healthy case too, which is the state your system is in 99.9% of the time: if partitions exist you trade consistency for availability, and otherwise you trade consistency for latency. One more nuance I would add in a design review: 'C' is scoped per operation, not per database. A single product can have a linearizable payment write, a majority-committed profile read, an eventually consistent like counter, and a linearizable admin permission check, all in the same deploy. The skill is knowing which data class cannot accept the 'A' branch of the trade-off."

interviewQuestions.text: What does PACELC add, and give a workload where you would accept staleness in a partition but not in the healthy case.
Explain linearizable vs sequential vs causal consistency, with a user-visible example of each.
"Eventually consistent" — what would you have to add to that sentence to make it engineerable?
How do stores expose consistency? Name the MongoDB, DynamoDB, and Cassandra knobs.
interviewQuestions.answer: "For MongoDB: readConcern of local or available (possibly stale), majority (majority-committed, and the default write concern pairs with it), linearizable (primary plus the most recent majority-committed data, at the cost of a round trip, and not usable in a transaction or against secondaries), and snapshot for a multi-document consistent read. Causal consistency is a session property. For DynamoDB, ConsistentRead: true on a table, doubling read capacity, which is unavailable on global secondary indexes and in some cross-region configurations. For Cassandra, ONE through ALL, plus the LOCAL_ variants, and the rule that the only thing protecting you from stale reads is the quorum math: R + W greater than the replication factor. I would expose consistency as a per-endpoint policy and log it, because 'eventually consistent' as a global label hides where the risk actually sits."

interviewQuestions.text: What is a failure detector, why can it not observe failure directly, and what does phi buy you?
Why must a lock be fenced, and how does a false failure detection turn into data loss without one?
Build a latency budget for a 200ms product page that fans out to Postgres, Redis, and Elasticsearch.
Requirement: seat booking with zero double-booking. Which store, and what consistency level per operation?
Requirement: social feed read by 50k users/sec. Which store, and what do you denormalize?
When is Postgres with `jsonb` and pgvector a better answer than five purpose-built services?

topics.title: BSON and _id
topics.description: BSON and _id within Database Systems: Additional Topics 19.
keyConcepts: BSON is a binary-encoded superset of JSON with explicit types: int32, int64, double, decimal128, date, timestamp, ObjectId, binary, regex, minKey/maxKey, undefined, symbol, DBPointer. int64 vs double matters: NumberLong avoids the 2^53 precision cliff that JavaScript numbers create for large counters, and NumberDecimal avoids binary floating-point money arithmetic. Never store money as double; use integer minor units or decimal128.

Type coercion traps in queries: { count: "5" } does not match { count: 5 } (except the numeric-type equivalence rules, where int, long, and double compare equal across types); { createdAt: "2026-01-01" } does not match a Date; true/1 do not match. Explicitly type your query values, because the driver's TypeScript types are not enforced at runtime by Mongo itself.

ObjectId is 12 bytes: a 4-byte seconds timestamp, a 5-byte per-process random value, and a 3-byte counter. Consequences: ids created by different processes interleave arbitrarily, so an _id range scan is *approximately* time-ordered (fine for coarse time buckets, not fine-grained ordering), and there is no global monotonicity. If you need true ordering or exactly-once-ish inserts from concurrent writers, use an application-generated sortable id (ULID/UUIDv7) or a sequence, and know that UUIDv7 is time-ordered but leaks creation time.
_id is always indexed and unique per collection. Uniqueness is per collection, not global, and a field named _id is immutable once set.

Key order matters for size and for compression because BSON is serialized in document order, and the server compacts documents for storage. Putting the most-frequently-read small fields first is a real, measurable micro-optimization for cache-resident documents.

topics.title: Indexes that matter, and the ESR rule
topics.description: Indexes that matter, and the ESR rule within Database Systems: Additional Topics 19.
keyConcepts: The ordering rules, stated properly
Put equality fields first. They are the most selective prefix and make the index reusable for any subset of the equalities as a prefix.
Then the sort field, so the index provides the ordering and no in-memory SORT stage is needed.
Then range fields. Once a range predicate appears, later fields in the index are no longer usable for bounding the scan (only for filtering), so they contribute little.
The index-cardinality pitfalls

Leading low-cardinality field is not automatically bad — for a *compound* index it is excellent, because the equality prefix still makes it selective overall ({ status: 1, createdAt: -1 } over millions of docs beats { createdAt: -1 } when you always filter on status).
Leading low-cardinality field in a single-field index is usually useless for point lookups: { deleted: 1 } matches half the collection. The index may still help a covered count or a sort.
Cardinality is not the whole story; size is. A field with 10 distinct values but 1KB strings costs more index space and more cache misses than a field with 100k distinct small values.

Low-cardinality sort fields are a trap. Sorting on status gives a poor plan; sorting on createdAt needs an index. If you genuinely need ordering by a low-cardinality field, include a tiebreaker in the compound index ({ status: 1, createdAt: -1 }) and sort by both.

Redundant indexes are pure cost. { a: 1 } is subsumed by { a: 1, b: 1 } for lookups on a; but { a: 1, b: 1 } cannot serve a sort on b alone, and { a: -1, b: 1 } is not redundant with { a: 1, b: 1 } because of the mixed direction. The sortKeys / index stats report is how you find these.
Each index is a second write path per document, plus memory pressure in the WiredTiger cache, plus a thing to remember at 3am. Index count per collection is a design metric.
Reading the explain output
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```js
db.orders.find({ tenantId: 't1', status: 'paid' })
       .sort({ createdAt: -1 })
       .explain('executionStats');
```

topics.title: Aggregation pipelines, real ones
topics.description: Aggregation pipelines, real ones within Database Systems: Additional Topics 19.
keyConcepts: The 100MB sort memory limit
Do not sort that much. Add an index that provides the sort, add a $match that narrows the input, or use $bucket/$group to aggregate down before sorting.
allowDiskUse: true on the aggregate call, which lets blocking stages spill to temporary files. It works, it is much slower, and it writes to the temp directory, so watch disk.
Raise the internal memory limit — viable in a self-managed deployment, but you are trading RAM for spill, so it needs capacity planning.

topics.title: Multi-document transactions
topics.description: Multi-document transactions within Database Systems: Additional Topics 19.
keyConcepts: What they cost and when they fail
A transaction requires a replica set (a standalone server cannot run one) and pins all reads and writes to one session and one primary.
Default read concern inside a transaction is snapshot; writes default to majority-ish behaviour. Both are deliberate, and both cost latency and throughput.

The transaction lifetime is bounded by the oplog window (60 minutes in modern releases; anything older aborts) and by transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds (default 60s). Never hold one open across user input.
Do not iterate a cursor inside a transaction; materialise the result with a bounded toArray or run the read outside. A large cursor plus a 60s ceiling is a guaranteed abort.

Write conflicts abort the whole transaction; withTransaction retries only errors carrying the TransientTransactionError label. A WriteConflict (code 112) under contention is normal and retryable; a plain DuplicateKey is not, and retrying it will not help.

No DDL for collections or indexes inside a transaction in the general case (creating collections and indexes is not allowed in a multi-document transaction; some collMod-style changes are). Schema changes go through a separate, coordinated step.
Cross-shard transactions are supported (two-phase commit across participants) with much higher latency and a large failure surface.
Do not nest transactions, and do not open two transactions on the same session.
Interview framing

topics.title: Read concerns, write concerns, read preference, causal sessions
topics.description: Read concerns, write concerns, read preference, causal sessions within Database Systems: Additional Topics 19.
keyConcepts: Read concern
Write concern

w: 0 = fire and forget (no ack at all; a rolled-back write looks successful). w: 1 = primary ack, which can still be rolled back on failover. w: "majority" = majority ack, which is what you want for anything you cannot reconstruct. w: <number> and tag-set w exist for custom quorums.

j: true additionally waits for the journal, which matters for node-level crash durability, not for replica failures. wtimeoutMS bounds the wait and *raises an error* — set it, and treat the error as "outcome unknown", not "failed", which means retry with the same idempotency key.

Every write should be retryable (retryWrites is on by default) and idempotent; that is what makes safe retries possible. Error codes worth recognizing: NotWritablePrimary / PrimarySteppedDown (retryable, the primary changed), WriteConflict (retryable), DuplicateKey (not retryable), UnknownTransactionCommitResult (commit, do not retry the whole thing).
Read preference
Causal sessions

topics.title: Sharding, replication, elections
topics.description: Sharding, replication, elections within Database Systems: Additional Topics 19.
keyConcepts: Replication and elections

electionTimeoutMillis (default 10000) must exceed the heartbeat period (default 2000) by a comfortable margin, and both must exceed your worst observed GC pause and network hiccup, or you get spurious elections.
priority: 0 marks a member as never-primary (read replicas). Pair that with hidden: true so reads are not routed to it.
tags drive read-preference routing, so a dc tag per member lets you pin reads to a region.
Plan maintenance with rs.freeze() (freeze elections for N seconds) before a node reboot, otherwise you cause an election and a write pause.

With w: "majority", acknowledged writes survive an election. With w: 1, an election can roll back a write the client was told succeeded. That is the single most important durability decision in a Mongo deployment.
Shard key selection — the decision that is expensive to reverse
The shard key must be immutable, never missing, and always indexed; a query without the shard key value hits every shard.
Prefer a key with high cardinality and even distribution matching your dominant query. Range keys cluster; hashed keys spread.

Chunk balancing: chunks (a shard key range's worth of data) are split when they exceed a size threshold, and the balancer moves chunks to equalize. Moves are online, and the balancer competes with production traffic, so you schedule it and can disable it per collection.

Targeted vs scatter-gather: a query containing the full shard key is *targeted* — one shard, low latency, and the index on that shard is fully effective. A query missing the shard key is *scatter-gather*: mongos fans out to every shard, each returns up to limit rows (so limit: 10 on a 20-shard cluster can pull 200 documents), each shard sorts in its own 100MB budget, and mongos performs a blocking merge sort to produce global ordering. Consequences: latency is the slowest shard, the sort memory limit applies, and a deep skip is brutal. EXPLAIN shows SHARD_MERGE and the sortPattern — if that sort is not your shard key, the query does not scale with cluster size.

Uniqueness and sharding: a unique index must be prefixed by the shard key. A bare unique index on _id is only unique per shard, not globally, because _id is not a globally ordered key. Choose a globally unique key or include the shard key.
commonMistakes: saying "MongoDB is schemaless" (it is schema-*flexible with validators*; dynamic typing is a feature and a migration hazard); embedding unbounded arrays; leading a compound index with a sort field before the equality prefix; running $lookup before $match; expecting a write to be searchable instantly (that is a search-engine property, not Mongo's — for Mongo, readConcern: linearizable); assuming w: 1 is durable; using ALLOW FILTERING-style full-partition reads (Cassandra, 6.21); shard keys chosen for write distribution while the dominant read omits the key; forgetting that a sharded collection's _id is not globally unique by default; treating change streams as a durable queue.
practiceTasks: model a posts + comments system in MongoDB three ways — naive embedded array, bucketed by day, and separate collection with a denormalized commentCount. For each, write the two real queries (feed page, post detail) with their pipelines, add the indexes, and measure with explain('executionStats') at 1M posts and 50M comments. Then insert a 60,000-element embedded array and watch the document approach the limit. Finally, implement a change-stream consumer with resume-token persistence and kill it for 90 seconds to see recovery behaviour.

interviewQuestions.text: What is BSON and why does it exist? Name three types JSON cannot express cleanly.
What is an `ObjectId` made of, and what ordering guarantees can you rely on?
Embed or reference: state the decision rules as a checklist.
interviewQuestions.answer: "My checklist is five questions. First, is the child bounded? If the array grows with time or user activity — comments, events, sessions, reviews — it is unbounded and must not be embedded, because it will hit the 16MB document limit and because a partial update rewrites the whole document. Second, is the child ever read without the parent? If I filter, sort, or paginate the child independently, it needs to be its own document with its own index, because I cannot page inside an array. Third, do the child and parent change together? If the child updates at a different rate or by a different service, embedding multiplies write amplification. Fourth, does atomicity matter? If the child must be consistent with the parent on every read, I either embed or I need a transaction, and a transaction is a design smell. Fifth, what is the total size and its growth? Under a few hundred small sub-documents, embedded is usually right. The pattern I fall back to for the unbounded case is bucketing: a parent holds pointers to bucket documents, each covering a time or id range, so the parent stays small and reads stay one or two round trips."
