topics.title: Redis data structures and what each one is for
topics.description: Redis data structures and what each one is for within Database Systems: Additional Topics 20.
keyConcepts: The mental model for choosing

topics.title: Single-threaded execution, pipelining, and blocking
topics.description: Single-threaded execution, pipelining, and blocking within Database Systems: Additional Topics 20.
keyConcepts: Redis executes commands on a single thread (with I/O threads in recent versions for reading and writing, and background threads for persistence and replication), so a single instance is *serialized by design*. That is why a Redis GET has a sub-millisecond p50 with no lock contention: there is no shared-nothing parallelism to coordinate.

The consequence is the failure mode: one slow command stalls every other client. A KEYS * on a 10M-key database, a huge HGETALL, a SORT without LIMIT, a SMEMBERS on a giant set, or Lua that loops a million times will block the event loop for hundreds of milliseconds. Use SCAN with COUNT instead of KEYS, SSCAN/HSCAN/ZSCAN instead of the blocking variants, and always bound SORT with LIMIT (or use ZRANGE).

Memory is the other single resource. Redis is in-memory: 100GB of data is 100GB of RAM plus overhead, and the allocator fragmentation plus copy-on-write during fork can double the footprint. This is why persistence (RDB snapshot) on a large dataset has a latency spike and why maxmemory policy decisions are an SRE conversation.

Pipelining sends many commands in one round trip, without waiting for individual replies. With network RTT at 0.3ms, 1000 sequential GETs cost 300ms; pipelined they cost about one RTT plus server time.

MULTI/EXEC is a transaction only in the narrowest sense: it guarantees the queued commands run in order without interleaving with other clients' commands. It does *not* roll back on error, it does not give isolation from reads outside the queue, and a WATCHed key changed by another client aborts the whole thing. Modern code usually prefers a single Lua script or a function, because one round trip and atomic execution beats queue-then-exec.
Real atomicity primitive: Lua scripts and functions, which execute atomically on the main thread. Keep them short; a long script is a long stall.

topics.title: Persistence, replication, Sentinel, Cluster
topics.description: Persistence, replication, Sentinel, Cluster within Database Systems: Additional Topics 20.
keyConcepts: Cluster errors you must know: MOVED <slot> <host:port> (the slot lives elsewhere permanently; a good client follows it and caches the mapping), ASK <slot> <host:port> (the slot is migrating; issue the command only against that node for this one request, do not cache), CROSSSLOT (a multi-key command or Lua script touched keys in different slots — fix it with hash tags: {user:42}:profile and {user:42}:prefs hash to the same slot), CLUSTERDOWN (not enough replicas covering enough slots to serve the requested consistency), TRYAGAIN/CLUSTERDOWN during resharding.
maxmemory and eviction. When memory hits maxmemory, Redis evicts per the configured maxmemory-policy, and this is a data-loss event for anything that is not rebuildable.
Two rules that save systems

topics.title: DynamoDB: keys, access-pattern-first design
topics.description: DynamoDB: keys, access-pattern-first design within Database Systems: Additional Topics 20.
keyConcepts: Two keys, both mandatory: a partition key (hash) and an optional sort key (range). The partition key must be an equality match — query requires it; a missing partition key means scan. The sort key supports =, begins_with, <, <=, >, >=, between, and the sortOrder variant of begins_with for pagination.

Design the table from the access patterns, not the entities. Write the queries first, then decide the key schema. This is the "access-pattern-first" discipline and the thing that makes a single-table design coherent.

Hot partitions. A single partition is hard-capped at 1,000 WCU/s and 1,000 RCU/s (with a 3,000 WCU/s write burst allowance in provisioned mode). One hot key means one third of your throughput regardless of table size. Diagnose with CloudWatch's SuccessfulRequestLatency and ThrottledRequests per partition, or by looking for one item dominating.

Projections and secondary indexes. A base table carries the full item. An LSI shares the base table's partition key and sort key capacity, costs no extra write capacity for maintenance, and only supports eventually consistent reads, but doubles the write I/O on disk. A GSI is a separate table with its own partition/sort key, consumes its own read and write capacity, supports only eventually consistent reads, and can be KEYS_ONLY, INCLUDE (a subset of non-key attributes), or ALL. GSIs are how you get more access patterns; they are also where the "eventually consistent read right after a write" surprise comes from.

Consistency. ConsistentRead: true costs 2x the RCU, is invalid on GSIs and LSIs, and is invalid on Global Tables secondaries. The failure mode to remember: a read immediately after a write, with ConsistentRead omitted, can return nothing at all for that key. Retrying fixes it; "the write is not there" is the symptom, not "the write failed".
Conditional writes are the correctness tool:

Capacity modes. Provisioned with auto scaling tracks utilization per dimension (WCU and RCU scale independently, target utilization configurable, 20% minimum floor) and is cheaper at steady state but can be throttled when growth outruns the scaling reaction. On-demand prices roughly 2x per unit but is right for spiky, unpredictable, or development traffic; the catch is a double-rate charge on sudden spikes above twice the trailing peak. Reserved capacity is for a known baseline.

TTL deletes an item after expiresAt on a number (epoch seconds); it is best effort, asynchronous, and may take up to 48 hours, so never treat TTL as a correctness mechanism — treat it as a garbage collector and make reads tolerate an item that has not yet vanished.

Streams give an ordered, at-least-once log of every write (24-hour retention) per shard, which is the basis for change-data capture into a warehouse, a search indexer, or a cache invalidator. StreamViewType of NEW_IMAGE, OLD_IMAGE, NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES, or KEYS_ONLY lets you pay only for what you need. The classic design problem: the DB and the stream are two copies of the truth, so every consumer must be idempotent and must handle the case where the stream lags behind the table (read from the table first if you need the latest state, then apply the event).

DAX is an in-memory micro-cache in front of DynamoDB: per-item micro-TTL (seconds), request collapsing, and a cluster of cache nodes up to 1TB each. It gives effectively consistent reads for hot items within the micro-TTL, cuts RCU cost dramatically for read-heavy skewed workloads, and needs DescribeTable permission or schema files for auto-discovery. It is read-only caching: it does not make writes faster, and it explicitly does not serve strongly consistent reads, so the "I read my own write through DAX" case still needs care.

topics.title: Caching patterns
topics.description: Caching patterns within Database Systems: Additional Topics 20.
keyConcepts: Cache-aside, the code that is actually right

TTL plus jitter is not optional at scale. Fixed TTLs loaded by a batch expire simultaneously and produce a periodic stampede; adding ±20% random jitter spreads expiry and reduces peak miss rate by a large factor.
Stampede protection, three techniques:
Single-flight (in-process): a map of in-flight promises per key; concurrent misses share one load. Cheapest and it fixes the single-process case.

Distributed lock: SET lock:key <token> NX PX 5000; the winner loads, others sleep briefly and retry the cache. Fixes the multi-process case. Needs a token-checked release (Lua, below) and a bounded wait, and the TTL must exceed the worst expected load time.
Early recompute: when an entry is within 20% of expiry, the *first* reader triggers the refresh while serving the current value. Turns a synchronized miss into a smooth trickle.

topics.title: Rate limiting: five algorithms and when each is right
topics.description: Rate limiting: five algorithms and when each is right within Database Systems: Additional Topics 20.
keyConcepts: Sliding window log
Sliding window counter
Token bucket
Leaky bucket
Cluster and multi-region caveats for rate limiting

A single Redis instance caps at ~100k ops/s; above that, shard the limiter keys across a cluster. Because each key is independent, this is easy — but the *global* limit is no longer exact; it becomes per-shard, so decide whether your SLA requires a global or per-shard limit.

Multi-region requires either a home-region limiter (extra cross-region latency on the check, and a hole if the region is down) or a per-region limiter (limit multiplied by regions — state it explicitly, and multiply your per-region limit by the number of regions so the global limit holds).

Fail open or fail closed, deliberately. For a login endpoint, fail closed. For a read endpoint, fail open and count it in metrics. Make it a config flag, and alert on it, because a fail-open flag left on during an incident is a very expensive mistake.

Counters drift under eviction. With allkeys-lru at capacity, limiter keys get evicted and every client effectively gets a fresh quota. Give the limiter instance noeviction and a headroom-based memory alert.
Sessions in Redis

You need to lose nothing. Redis is in-memory and its durability is a background job. If a region dies and a replica promotes, you can lose the last second (AOF everysec) or the last acknowledged writes (async replication). min-replicas-to-write + WAIT narrows the window; it does not close it.
You need transactions with real isolation. MULTI/EXEC is not a transaction in the ACID sense. Multi-key invariants need a single document (hash with fields) plus a Lua script, or a real database.
commonMistakes: using KEYS in production code; storing large values in Redis; mixing cache and authoritative data in one instance with allkeys-lru; assuming MULTI/EXEC rolls back; using a fixed TTL for every key; releasing a lock with a plain DEL; believing Redlock gives you exactly-once side effects; using a fixed window for a hard quota; passing Date.now() from inside the Lua script and losing control of clock skew; assuming DynamoDB Query can filter across partitions; expecting an eventually consistent read to return a just-written item; using FilterExpression to "reduce" Scan cost (it does not); putting high-cardinality, unbounded values in a limiter or cache keyspace without bounds.
practiceTasks: implement all five rate limiters in TypeScript against a local Redis, plus an in-process variant, and write a load test that hammers the boundary: send exactly limit requests at the end of a fixed window, then limit at the start of the next, and plot which algorithms let 2x through. Then convert the token bucket to use a distributed lock plus a "leader refreshes, followers wait" pattern, and show the failure mode when the leader dies. Finally, set maxmemory 64mb on a scratch instance, fill it, and watch each eviction policy do its thing.

// rate: 100/minute
const key = `rl:fixed:${userId}:${Math.floor(Date.now() / 60_000)}`;
const n = await redis.incr(key);

```ts
const LUA_LOG = `
local key      = KEYS[1]
local now      = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local window   = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local limit    = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local member   = ARGV[4]
redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', key, '-inf', now - window)
local used = redis.call('ZCARD', key)
if used >= limit then
  local oldest = redis.call('ZRANGE', key, 0, 0, 'WITHSCORES')
  local retry = 0
  if oldest[2] then retry = math.ceil(tonumber(oldest[2]) + window - now) end
  redis.call('PEXPIRE', key, window)
  return { 0, used, retry }
end
redis.call('ZADD', key, now, member)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', key, window)
return { 1, used + 1, 0 }
`;

async function slidingLog(userId: string, limit = 10, windowMs = 60_000) {
  const now = Date.now();
  const member = `${now}-${crypto.randomUUID()}`;   // unique: same-ms writes must not overwrite
  const [allowed, used, retryMs] = await redis.eval(
    LUA_LOG, 1, `rl:log:${userId}`, now, windowMs, limit, member
  ) as [number, number, number];
  return { allowed: allowed === 1, used, retryAfterMs: retryMs };
}
```

```ts
const LUA_SWC = `
local now    = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local w      = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local limit  = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local start  = now - (now % w)

local function read(k)
  local r = redis.call('HMGET', k, 's', 'c')
  local s, c = tonumber(r[1]), tonumber(r[2])
  if s == nil then return nil, 0 end
  return s, c
end

local cs, cc = read(KEYS[1])
local ps, pc = read(KEYS[2])

if cs ~= start then
  if cs == start - w then
    pc = cc                 -- the old current window becomes the previous one
  else
    pc = 0                  -- a gap: nothing in the trailing window
  end
  cc = 0
  redis.call('DEL', KEYS[2])
  redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 's', start, 'c', 0)
end

local elapsed = (now - start) / w
local est = cc + pc * (1 - elapsed)

if est >= limit then
  redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], w * 2)
  redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[2], w * 2)
  return { 0, tostring(est) }
end

cc = cc + 1
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 's', start, 'c', cc)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], w * 2)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[2], w * 2)
return { 1, tostring(est + 1) }
`;

async function slidingCounter(userId: string, limit = 100, windowMs = 60_000) {
  // Hash tags keep both keys in one slot so the script is Cluster-safe.
  const base = `rl:swc:{${userId}}`;
  const res = await redis.eval(LUA_SWC, 2, `${base}:c`, `${base}:p`,
                              Date.now(), windowMs, limit) as [number, string];
  return { allowed: res[0] === 1, estimate: Number(res[1]), limit };
}
```

```ts
const LUA_TB = `
local key      = KEYS[1]
local now      = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[2])   -- max burst
local rate     = tonumber(ARGV[3])   -- tokens per millisecond

local data   = redis.call('HMGET', key, 't', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(data[1])
local ts     = tonumber(data[2])
if tokens == nil then tokens = capacity; ts = now end

local delta = now - ts
if delta < 0 then delta = 0 end               -- clock moved backwards: do not grant tokens
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + delta * rate)

local allowed, retry = 0, 0
if tokens >= 1 then
  allowed, tokens = 1, tokens - 1
else
  retry = math.ceil((1 - tokens) / rate)
end

redis.call('HSET', key, 't', tostring(tokens), 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', key, math.ceil(capacity / rate) + 1000)
return { allowed, tostring(tokens), retry }
`;

async function tokenBucket(userId: string, { capacity = 20, perSecond = 5 } = {}) {
  const res = await redis.eval(LUA_TB, 1, `rl:tb:${userId}`,
    Date.now(), capacity, perSecond / 1000) as [number, string, number];
  return { allowed: res[0] === 1, tokens: Number(res[1]), retryAfterMs: res[2] };
}
```

topics.title: The data model that makes it fast
topics.description: The data model that makes it fast within Database Systems: Additional Topics 21.
keyConcepts: Partition key (device_id) chooses which node owns the data. All rows with the same partition key live on the same set of replicas, so a query touching only the partition key needs no cross-node coordination.
Clustering columns (day, ts) order rows *within* a partition and let you slice a range: WHERE device_id = ? AND ts > ? reads one contiguous span.

Rules that follow: every query must specify the partition key. The clustering columns must be constrained in prefix order — you can range on ts only if you also constrain day, because the data is sorted by (day, ts). Partition size is the tuning parameter that matters most: a 1GB partition makes reads slow and unrepairable, a 10MB partition wastes memory on the read path.
Static columns hold a value that is not per-row but per-partition (a device's metadata). One write, cached with the partition, no extra row.

Collections (set, list, map) exist and are convenient for small, bounded, rarely-queried data. They are a well-known footgun: multi-cell reads, poor compaction, and a poor fit for queries that need to search inside. Use them for a handful of tags, not for a list of 10,000 events.

Materialized views are the escape valve for "I need a second query shape": a view with a different primary key, written asynchronously from the base table. It is eventual, it costs double the write path, and it is still a whole table you must model. In practice, most Cassandra schemas use several *tables* per entity rather than views.
One table per query, denormalized

topics.title: ALLOW FILTERING and secondary indexes: the traps
topics.description: ALLOW FILTERING and secondary indexes: the traps within Database Systems: Additional Topics 21.
keyConcepts: SELECT * FROM t WHERE partition = 'x' AND non_key_column = 'y' ALLOW FILTERING reads every row of the partition, discards most of them, and returns the rest. The coordinator needs heap for the whole partition, the read time is proportional to partition size, and a concurrent write storm makes it worse. It is a debugging tool, and in production it is a self-inflicted outage on a schedule.

Secondary indexes (2i) do exist, and they are not a general answer: they are local to each node (so a query with a secondary-index predicate fans out to all replicas and merges), they can return inconsistent results under concurrency, they do not scale with data volume, and they multiply write cost. Use them for a genuinely low-selectivity filter; otherwise denormalize.
SASI indexes and the newer storage-attached indexes improve on some of this but do not change the philosophy: *design for the query you know*.

topics.title: Consistency, quorum maths, and repair
topics.description: Consistency, quorum maths, and repair within Database Systems: Additional Topics 21.
keyConcepts: Levels: ONE, TWO, THREE, QUORUM, ALL, EACH_QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, LOCAL_ONE, LOCAL_SERIAL, SERIAL.
The arithmetic you must be able to do out loud: for replication factor N, QUORUM = floor(N/2) + 1. With N = 3: ONE = 1, QUORUM = 2, ALL = 3.

The anti-entropy rule: for a read/write to be *strongly* consistent you need R + W > N. With N = 3, W = 2 and R = 2 guarantees the read and write sets overlap in at least one replica, so a read cannot miss a committed write.

W > N/2 is what stops lost updates and phantom data from an acknowledged write that is then "unwritten" by a stale coordinator. W = 1 with N = 3 means two replicas can disagree with the ack forever (until a repair), and a client that got a success has no guarantee.

Stale reads are legitimate and cheap at ONE; the trap is using ONE for a read that must reflect a just-acknowledged write. The fix is a read-your-writes token: a per-client monotonically increasing timestamp captured on write (UPDATE ... USING TIMESTAMP ?), then a read with a "cluster" or "client" timestamp filter that refuses anything older. Cassandra's USING TIMESTAMP is also how you do last-write-wins conflict resolution, and the clock is the client's, so clock skew becomes your problem — bound it with a coarse per-client timestamp, and be honest that skewed clocks can lose writes.

Read repair happens on reads at QUORUM or higher: mismatched replicas are fixed in the background. ONE reads skip it, so a ONE-read-heavy workload accumulates divergence; that is why nodetool repair is a scheduled, non-optional operational task.

Hinted handoff is how a write survives a replica being down: the coordinator stores a hint and delivers it when the node returns. It is bounded by the down-time you can tolerate, and after gc_grace (default 10 days) hints and tombstones are dropped, so a replica that is down too long needs a full nodetool repair or a rebuild from a snapshot.

Tombstones and gc_grace: a delete is a tombstone, not a removal, and it is a *write* that must be broadcast. Heavy delete workloads create large tombstone counts; a read touching too many tombstones fails with tombstone count exceeds threshold. The gc_grace window is the price of a distributed delete, and lowering it for write-heavy data can resurrect deleted rows on a late-arriving replica.

LWT (lightweight transactions): INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS gives you a compare-and-set *within a single partition* at SERIAL consistency, at the cost of roughly two round trips (a prepare phase and a commit phase) and a paxos-like agreement. It is the correct tool for "this username must be unique" and "check-then-act on a counter". It is *not* a transaction across partitions and it is *not* free: heavy LWT usage serialises on the partition and destroys throughput. Use it where a uniqueness constraint genuinely cannot be expressed otherwise.

topics.title: Compaction, TTLs, and operations
topics.description: Compaction, TTLs, and operations within Database Systems: Additional Topics 21.
keyConcepts: Compaction is where SSTables get merged and where reads get fast. STCS (size-tiered) is the default: good for write-heavy and uniform data, bad for read latency spikes and for data with uneven per-partition sizes. LCS (leveled) gives lower read amplification at the cost of write amplification and more compaction work. TWCS (time-window) is the right choice for time-series data with TTLs, because it buckets by time window and drops whole expired buckets cheaply. Choosing the compaction strategy for the access pattern (write-heavy vs read-heavy, uniform vs skewed, TTL or not) is a genuinely senior decision.
Compression (LZ4 by default, or a heavier algorithm) trades CPU for space and I/O, and it is nearly always worth it.

TTL is per row (USING TTL ?) or per table (default_time_to_live). Expiry is not exact: it happens during compaction of the bucket, so a row can outlive its TTL by minutes or hours, and it generates tombstones that participate in gc_grace. TTLs also make a node unreachable for a period ("UNREACHABLE" for 2x TTL after an extended outage) because re-inserting a row whose tombstone is still around can resurrect data. Plan node-down time against your TTL.

A write path worth understanding: client → coordinator → memtable (in memory) → SSTable on disk, with an in-memory row cache and a bloom filter per SSTable to avoid reading files that cannot contain the key. Bloom filters are why a missing key in a large partition is cheap, and why ALLOW FILTERING is not: a filter on a *non-key* column has no bloom filter to consult.

Capacity and distribution: virtual nodes spread a token's ownership across many nodes so adding a node does not require moving a huge contiguous range. Reads follow the token ring; the coordinator is chosen by the partitioner. Nothing is a single point of failure, but every write is replicated N ways, so the storage amplification is real.

topics.title: When Cassandra fits
topics.description: When Cassandra fits within Database Systems: Additional Topics 21.
keyConcepts: Fits
Very high write ingest where a write is a local append: IoT telemetry, event/click logs, audit trails, messaging metadata.
A small, *known* set of queries, stated in advance, with a bounded partition size.
Time-ordered data with retention (telemetry, activity feeds), especially with TWCS and TTLs.
Multi-datacentre replication with region-local reads and no cross-region coordination on the write path.
A team that accepts denormalization as a permanent architectural commitment.
Does not fit
Ad-hoc exploration, reporting, or "one more question" work. There is no join, no group-by across partitions, and no ad-hoc index.
Read-heavy relational workloads with many secondary lookups.
Transactions spanning entities (a transfer between two accounts). Use a single ledger row, or a relational store.
Small data. A single-node Cassandra cluster has more operational surface than a Postgres table, and no benefit.
A team that wants transactions. Full stop.
commonMistakes: designing the schema around entities instead of queries; forgetting clustering columns must be constrained in prefix order; using ALLOW FILTERING in a "temporary" fix; assuming a unique constraint is free (it needs an LWT or a denormalized uniqueness table); treating a TTL as precise; ignoring gc_grace when planning node downtime; believing W = 1 is fine because "the coordinator acked"; assuming secondary indexes are equivalent to a relational index.
practiceTasks: load 50M rows into a three-node cluster with a 10-day TTL. Measure insert throughput at ONE, QUORUM, and LOCAL_QUORUM; then measure read p99 at each level and the effect of compaction strategy on read latency. Kill a node mid-write and observe hinted handoff, then leave it down past gc_grace and see what a repair has to do. Finally, write a query you *want* but did not model, and time the ALLOW FILTERING version against a materialized-view version.

interviewQuestions.text: What is a partition key versus a clustering column, and how do they differ in a query?
What happens to `WHERE device_id = ? AND ts > ?` if `day` is a clustering column before `ts`?
Why must every query specify the partition key?
How do you choose a partition size, and what goes wrong at 1GB?
What is the "one table per query" pattern, and what does it cost?
What are static columns for?
Why is `ALLOW FILTERING` dangerous? Explain the mechanism.
What are the problems with secondary indexes in Cassandra?
Define the consistency levels and compute `QUORUM` for `N = 5`.
State the `R + W > N` rule and what breaks without it.
interviewQuestions.answer: "The rule is that for a read to be guaranteed to see any acknowledged write, the read replica set and the write replica set must overlap, and that happens when reads plus writes exceeds the replication factor. With three replicas, writing at quorum and reading at quorum gives four against three, so there is at least one node in both sets and the read cannot miss the write. The failure case is instructive: write at ONE, read at ONE. The client writes to replica A, is acknowledged, then reads from replica B, which has not received the write yet, and gets stale data from a write that was reported as successful. Worse, if the coordinator for a later write is B, it can hand out a value that contradicts A, and because nothing repairs without a quorum read, the divergence persists. That is why the choice of write consistency is the durability decision, and why read consistency is a separate, per-query decision: the write path's W is what you promise, and the read path's R is what your users will actually see."

topics.title: Modelling
topics.description: Modelling within Database Systems: Additional Topics 22.
keyConcepts: Nodes carry identity and a label; edges carry direction, type, and usually properties (since, weight, role, validFrom). Labels should be few and meaningful; a property that is really a subclass is a label. A node with a type field (kind: 'a' | 'b') is harder to index and constrain than two labels.

Every relationship needs an identity of its own if you will ever attach properties or query it independently, and you need *both* directions queried, because an undirected traversal in a directed model requires two patterns or a flag. Modelling every edge as both (a)-[:X]->(b) and (b)-[:X]->(a) is a common and effective denormalization.
Edge properties must not be the only copy of the truth. A FRIENDSHIP edge with weight derived from interactions is a cache; it needs a rebuild path.

Nodes with too many edges (god nodes) destroy traversal performance and are usually a modelling smell — an "everything" supernode usually wants to be a set, a property, or a hyperedge split into an intermediate node.

Hyperedges (a relationship between a *set* of things: "these three people were in the same transaction") need an intermediate node, because a relationship in a property graph connects exactly two nodes.
Delete semantics: deleting a node requires deleting or nullifying every incident edge. In Neo4j that is DETACH DELETE, and the "orphan edge" question is a real interview detail.

topics.title: Cypher and traversal cost
topics.description: Cypher and traversal cost within Database Systems: Additional Topics 22.
keyConcepts: Cost model: a variable-length pattern is a breadth- or depth-first expansion with pruning. *1..4 over a node with 5,000 edges is up to 5^4 expansions before the LIMIT helps you. Mitigation: always bound depth, always LIMIT, put the selective predicate inside the traversal (-[r:FOLLOWS*1..3 WHERE r.since > ...]-) rather than filtering after, and put the LIMIT early where the engine can push it down.
Plans are cached per query shape, so parameterised Cypher is fast and string-built Cypher is not. This is the same lesson as prepared statements everywhere else.
Property existence in a WHERE on a hot traversal prevents cheap index use; index the node property you start from, and index edges you filter on.
Aggregation in Cypher is done in the engine, which is genuinely nice for graph-shaped aggregations that SQL cannot express cleanly.

topics.title: Relational alternatives that often win
topics.description: Relational alternatives that often win within Database Systems: Additional Topics 22.
keyConcepts: Interview framing
commonMistakes: using a graph store for one- and two-hop joins; unbounded * traversals; filtering after the traversal instead of inside it; string-concatenated Cypher; storing the only copy of data on an edge; not bounding depth; assuming a graph store gives you transactions across the whole graph, or foreign keys, or good reporting; forgetting that deleting a node leaves orphan edges unless you DETACH DELETE.
practiceTasks: take 100k synthetic users with a follows graph and answer the same three questions in Postgres (join table plus recursive CTE) and in a graph engine: (a) mutual connections of a user, (b) users within 3 hops who do not follow anyone I follow, (c) the size of the connected component. Record query times, memory, and the code length. Then try the same with depth unbounded to see exactly where both approaches stop being acceptable.

interviewQuestions.text: When is a graph database genuinely the right tool? Give three domains and one anti-example.
interviewQuestions.answer: "I reach for a graph when two things are true at once: the traversal depth is unbounded or unknown at design time, and the relationship itself is a first-class thing with data on it. Fraud ring detection is the canonical case — you ask who shares a device, a billing address, or a card BIN with whom, and you do not know in advance how far the ring extends; the query is a path query, and every hop is a comparison. Dependency and blast-radius analysis is the same shape: given this package, what breaks if it goes away. Recommendations by mutual connections are a three-hop traversal with an exclusion predicate, which is awkward in SQL and one line in Cypher. The anti-example is 'customers joined to their most recent order', which is a one-hop join with an index and a DISTINCT ON; a graph store there is overhead, loses foreign keys and transactions, and adds an engine to operate. So my rule is: fixed depth and no edge data means a join table, and I say that in the interview even when the question is dressed up in graph vocabulary."

topics.referenceMarkdown:
```sql
-- A join table is the right model for a fixed 1-hop relationship
CREATE TABLE follows (
  follower_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  followee_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id)
);
CREATE INDEX ON follows (followee_id);           -- reverse direction
-- A user with 10k followers:
SELECT u.* FROM users u JOIN follows f ON f.followee_id = $1
WHERE f.follower_id IN (SELECT id FROM users WHERE ...) LIMIT 50;
```

```sql
-- Variable depth via a recursive CTE, with a hard depth cap and a cycle guard
WITH RECURSIVE reach(user_id, depth, path) AS (
  SELECT $1::bigint, 0, ARRAY[$1::bigint]
  UNION ALL
  SELECT f.followee_id, r.depth + 1, r.path || f.followee_id
  FROM reach r
  JOIN follows f ON f.follower_id = r.user_id
  WHERE r.depth < 3
    AND NOT f.followee_id = ANY(r.path)          -- no revisits
)
SELECT user_id, MIN(depth) AS depth FROM reach GROUP BY user_id;
```

topics.title: TimescaleDB: hypertables and continuous aggregates
topics.description: TimescaleDB: hypertables and continuous aggregates within Database Systems: Additional Topics 23.
keyConcepts: What a hypertable gives you: automatic chunking by time so the index stays small and recent, chunk-local compression with a segment-by column (dictionaries for the low-cardinality part and delta-of-delta time encoding for the rest), retention as a DROP CHUNK instead of a mass DELETE, and the ability to attach custom retention and compression policies.

start_offset and end_offset matter for correctness, not just cost. An aggregate that refreshes every bucket up to "now" will keep recomputing the incomplete current bucket, and late-arriving data will be lost. Leaving end_offset at a few buckets means the most recent window is read from raw data, so out-of-order writes land correctly.

Continuous aggregates are incrementally refreshed — only the changed region is recomputed — which is what makes them cheap. They are read-only; refresh them with CALL refresh_continuous_aggregate(...). They are not real-time-accurate to the millisecond, and they *cannot* be joined against a raw hypertable in the same query in some versions, which is a real limitation to know before you design around them.
time_bucket_gapfill interpolates missing buckets so a chart does not draw a line through a device outage as if it were zero. Reporting a gap as 0 is a correctness bug that dashboards love to hide.

Watch out for: queries that join a hypertable to a normal table (the planner often does a hash join over the *entire* hypertable unless you filter by time first), the absence of a primary key in the Postgres sense on a hypertable (a unique index must include all partitioning columns), and ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 20 on a huge hypertable if the chunk pruning is not working. Always add an explicit time predicate and confirm chunk pruning with EXPLAIN.

Scale-out path: continuous aggregates roll up; beyond one node, use a columnar store (ClickHouse) or a warehouse. The honest answer is that Postgres-plus-Timescale is excellent up to a few hundred million rows per hypertable with good time predicates, and a columnar OLAP engine is better past that.
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS timescaledb;

-- a hypertable is one logical table auto-partitioned on the time column
SELECT create_hypertable('sensor_reading', by_range('ts'), if_not_exists => TRUE);

-- space partitioning on a second dimension buys parallelism and index locality
SELECT add_dimension('sensor_reading', by_hash('device_id', 8));

ALTER TABLE sensor_reading SET (
  timescaledb.compress,
  timescaledb.compress_segmentby = 'device_id',
  timescaledb.compress_orderby   = 'ts DESC'
);

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW sensor_hourly
WITH (timescaledb.continuous) AS
SELECT device_id,
       time_bucket('1 hour', ts) AS bucket,
       avg(value) AS avg_value,
       max(value) AS max_value
FROM sensor_reading
WHERE ts > now() - INTERVAL '7 days'
GROUP BY device_id, bucket
WITH NO DATA;                       -- build later, so the migration is fast

SELECT add_continuous_aggregate_policy('sensor_hourly',
  start_offset      => INTERVAL '30 days',   -- how far back it stays current
  end_offset        => INTERVAL '1 hour',    -- leave the last hour raw for late data
  schedule_interval => INTERVAL '10 minutes');

SELECT add_retention_policy('sensor_reading', INTERVAL '90 days');
```

topics.title: Prometheus TSDB: the cardinality trap
topics.description: Prometheus TSDB: the cardinality trap within Database Systems: Additional Topics 23.
keyConcepts: A series is a unique label set, and every series needs a chunk in memory, an index entry, and file space. The label set is the primary key, so labels are columns and their values are the cardinality multiplier: job, instance, and status give you 3 dimensions; adding user_id turns "a few thousand series" into "tens of millions" and the TSDB falls over. The rule: never use a high-cardinality value as a label. Push the id into the *value* as a field, or aggregate it out, or drop it.

The head block lives in memory/WAL and the checkpoint controls it: --storage.tsdb.max-block-duration, the head chunk range, and --storage.tsdb.head-chunks-write-queue-size interact so that a burst of series can OOM the process. Cap series with max_label_names_per_series and monitor prometheus_tsdb_head_series.

The scrape target count multiplies series: series ≈ targets × jobs × label combinations. Doubling the fleet doubles memory, which is why horizontal sharding (one Prometheus per team, or a Thanos/Cortex-style store) is the standard answer.

Recording rules pre-aggregate so dashboards query cheap series, and downsampling keeps long-range resolution affordable. Both are the correct answer to "we need 13 months of data" and both cost a rule-evaluation and a compaction story.
histogram_quantile over a high-cardinality le bucket set is expensive; recording rules that pre-aggregate the histogram into a quantile reduce the load.

Remote write is how you get durability and long retention (to a receiver or an object store), at the cost of batching, ordering not being guaranteed across shards, and duplicate series on a retry. Version the write request to avoid clobbering newer samples with out-of-order ones.

Contrast: InfluxDB's line protocol makes the same point differently — tags are indexed and are your series key, fields are values; putting a high-cardinality value in a tag is the same mistake under a different name.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

-- 1536-dim embeddings from a 1536-dim model
CREATE TABLE doc_chunk (
  id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  doc_id      bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES doc(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  tenant_id   bigint NOT NULL,
  content     text   NOT NULL,
  embedding   vector(1536) NOT NULL,
  model       text   NOT NULL,          -- pin the model that produced these vectors
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- HNSW: graph-based, high recall, high memory, slow build
CREATE INDEX doc_chunk_hnsw ON doc_chunk
  USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
  WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);

-- IVFFlat: inverted file, fast build, lower recall, needs a representative dataset
CREATE INDEX doc_chunk_ivf ON doc_chunk
  USING ivfflat (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
  WITH (lists = 1000);

SET hnsw.ef_search = 100;                 -- runtime recall/latency dial (session or per-role)
SET ivfflat.probes = 50;                  -- runtime dial for IVF
```

```sql
-- filtered search: the filter runs *after* the index scan, so selectivity decides your recall
SELECT d.id, d.doc_id, d.content,
       1 - (d.embedding <=> $1::vector) AS cosine_similarity
FROM doc_chunk d
WHERE d.tenant_id = $2                      -- hard filter, must be applied
  AND d.created_at > now() - interval '1 year'
ORDER BY d.embedding <=> $1::vector
LIMIT 20;
```

topics.title: TypeORM and Sequelize: the decorator generations
topics.description: TypeORM and Sequelize: the decorator generations within Database Systems: Additional Topics 24.
keyConcepts: TypeORM

Strengths: decorators give you a rich metadata model, it works across Postgres/MySQL/SQLite/Mongo, DataSource is a real configuration object, @AfterLoad/@BeforeInsert hooks are convenient, and the QueryBuilder is a complete escape hatch.

Drawbacks: the decorator + emitDecoratorMetadata setup is a compiler-configuration dependency; the entity metadata graph is hydrated at bootstrap (a real cost with hundreds of entities and a notorious source of slow test start-up); relations: { customer: true } in a loop is N+1; lazy relations were historically Promise<T> in some versions which changes typing everywhere; synchronize: true (schema auto-sync) will happily drop columns and must never be used against anything you care about; and the generated SQL is harder to predict than Drizzle's or Prisma's.
When to choose it: an existing codebase, a team already fluent in it, or a multi-dialect requirement that justifies the abstraction.
Sequelize
Strengths: mature, paranoid soft deletes, model and association hooks that are genuinely useful, and a well-known escape hatch to raw SQL.

Drawbacks: association include silently produces N+1 unless you use separate: true; Op symbol comparisons are verbose; group + attributes: [[fn('COUNT', col('id')), 'count']] is clunky; sync({ alter: true }) is destructive; and the general experience is "I am fighting the ORM" more often than with Prisma or Drizzle.

Hooks (beforeBulkCreate, afterCreate, afterFind) are the feature people miss: they are the natural place for audit stamping, but they fire per row on bulkCreate, so an N+1 log write is one keystroke away.

topics.title: The repository pattern, honestly
topics.description: an interface (or abstract class) in the domain layer that the rest of the code depends on, with a database-backed implementation and, usually, an in-memory one for tests.
keyConcepts: When it earns its keep
Testability without a database. A unit test for business logic runs in 1ms with an in-memory double instead of 300ms against a container. This is the strongest argument and it is real.
The domain stays free of the ORM. No Prisma types in the domain, so you can change persistence without touching business rules. This matters at the boundary of a large codebase.
Multiple backends or migrations in flight (a strangler-fig migration from one store to another, or a test-time in-memory substitute).
A stable, mockable seam for a large team where "how do I get the user's email" has one answer.
A place to put the transaction boundary and the unit of work, so callers cannot accidentally do half a unit of work.
When it is pure indirection
One backend, forever, and a team of ten or fewer. You have added a file, a mapping function, and a layer of indirection with no new capability.
The mapping tax: every repository method converts rows to domain objects, and that conversion is code you must write, test, and keep in sync. If the mapping is a rename per field, it is pure cost.

It hides power. The moment you need a window function, a LATERAL join, or a lock, the repository interface either grows a leaky method or you reach around it. A repository that has a method per query is a query builder with ceremony.
It becomes a "one repository per table" dumping ground, which is the classic failure. A repository should be shaped by *use cases* and return *aggregates*, not mirror tables row by row.
A generic BaseRepository<T> with findAll, findById, delete gives you type safety and zero design.
commonMistakes: creating a client per request; running migrate dev in production; sync({alter: true}) against real data; concatenating a sort column into SQL; a module-level DataLoader that leaks data between users; Promise.all inside an interactive transaction expecting parallelism; putting an HTTP call inside a transaction; long interactive transactions holding a pool connection; expanding and contracting in one deploy; CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY on a hot table; a BaseRepository<T> that mirrors tables; forgetting to set lock_timeout in migration sessions.

Then write a migration that adds a NOT NULL column with a default to a 10M-row table and prove, with EXPLAIN and by watching concurrent writes, that the add is instant and the SET DEFAULT step is the one that blocks. Finally, implement a repository interface with a Postgres and an in-memory implementation and measure how much the unit-test suite slows down without it.

topics.title: The inverted index, tokenization, and analyzers
topics.description: The inverted index, tokenization, and analyzers within Database Systems: Additional Topics 25.
keyConcepts: Inverted index: a map from term to a sorted list of documents containing it. Document-at-a-time scoring walks the postings and accumulates; term-at-a-time scoring iterates the dictionary and merges. Position data ("positions" in the posting) is what makes phrase queries and phrase proximity possible, at extra storage cost.

The analysis chain decides what a term *is*, and it is the biggest lever on search quality: character filters (strip HTML, asciifolding so "café" matches "cafe", a mapping filter for units or synonyms) → a tokenizer (standard, whitespace, ngram, pattern, language-specific ones) → token filters (lowercase, stop-word removal, stemming or lemmatization, synonym_graph, edge_ngram for autocomplete).

The classic surprise: the index is analyzed one way and the query is analyzed another. If the index uses a stemmer, the query must too, or "running" will never match "run". Same for asciifolding and synonyms. This is the number-one cause of "the search is broken for this one term", and the fix is usually the search_analyzer on the field.

keyword vs text: text is analyzed into terms and is not aggregatable or sortable. keyword is stored whole, unanalyzed, and is aggregatable, sortable, and exactly matchable. The standard pattern is a multi-field: "title": { "type": "text", "fields": { "raw": { "type": "keyword" } } } so you get full-text on title and exact/aggregatable title.raw.

Synonyms are a deployment event, not a config event. Changing a synonym file changes the analysis of the whole index, so you either reindex or use a *search-time* synonym set (a synonym_graph filter on a search_analyzer only), which is why search-time synonyms exist at all. Rule: never put a phrase in a plain synonym filter (a synonym_graph supports multi-word); keep synonyms in version control with tests; and expect relevance to move when you change them.

edge_ngram with min_gram: 2, max_gram: 15 on a search_as_you_type-style subfield gives prefix completion ("re" → "red running"). The cost is index size, and you should cap max_gram and only index the subfield, not the original.

topics.title: Relevance: TF-IDF, BM25, boosts, and decay
topics.description: Relevance: TF-IDF, BM25, boosts, and decay within Database Systems: Additional Topics 25.
keyConcepts: TF-IDF: score = tf * idf where idf = log(N / df). Intuition: a term that appears in nearly every document tells you nothing (common), a rare term tells you a lot. Plain TF explodes on long documents, so it is always normalised.
BM25 (the default in Lucene/Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) fixes the normalisation and adds term-frequency saturation:
Field boosts encode editorial judgement: title^5, tags^3, body^1. Boost the field where the term is more meaningful.

Recency decay for feeds and news: a function_score with gauss or exp on a date field, so a 3-hour-old match beats a 3-week-old match with the same text score. Do this in the query, not by mixing a timestamp into the text.

Score combination: bool queries with must (participates in scoring and is required), should (participates in scoring, optional, and needs minimum_should_match when combined with must), and filter (does *not* score, is cacheable, and is the right place for tenant, permission, and status predicates). Putting filters in filter clauses rather than must is the single biggest relevance-and-latency win in a filtered search: the filter cache can skip the whole clause.
Query-type cheat sheet

topics.title: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch internals you must know
topics.description: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch internals you must know within Database Systems: Additional Topics 25.
keyConcepts: Shard and replica. An index is split into primary shards (fixed at creation, so pick the number with growth in mind: bytes(primary) * shard_count should fit comfortably in a node, and too many shards means too many small Lucene segments and expensive merges). Each primary has N replicas, which provide redundancy and read capacity. Writes go to the primary, then are replicated. Reads go to primaries and replicas by default; you can send a read to a replica with preference.

The near-real-time model. This is the single most important operational fact: a write is not searchable until the next refresh (default 1s), which creates a new Lucene segment and opens it for search. So POST /index/_doc followed immediately by a search can return nothing. Mitigations: ?refresh=wait_for (wait for the next refresh, used in tests and for read-your-write flows) or ?refresh=true (force it now, at a cost — never on a write path). A bulk indexer should use the default refresh and accept up to 1s of lag.

Refresh interval trade-off: 1s means near-real-time search and more segments (more merge work, more heap, slower old-segment reads). 30s or -1 (manual) means a much more efficient, less search-eligible index. Use a long refresh or manual refresh for a reindex-from-scratch or a logs index.
_source vs doc values vs a stored field:

Mapping vs dynamic mapping. A mapping defines fields and their types. By default Elasticsearch *guesses* types from the first document it sees: "2026-01-01" becomes a date, "true" becomes a boolean, a numeric-looking string becomes a long. This is a genuine source of outages (a field that is sometimes a number and sometimes a string is a mapping conflict the first time, and then the *entire* indexing request for that shard fails). Controls: dynamic: "strict" (reject anything unmapped — best for correctness), dynamic: "false" (ignore unknown fields, keep them in _source), or dynamic_templates (route by pattern: all *_id to keyword, all *_at to date).

keyword vs text revisited with a decision rule: if you will ever sort, aggregate, filter exactly, or join on the field, it must be keyword. If you will ever full-text search it, it needs a text field. Fields that are *only* used for filtering should be keyword (cheap, no analysis). And a keyword field's ignore_above (commonly 256) means longer values are indexed as *not indexed* but still stored in _source — a silent truncation that breaks aggregations.

Mapping explosion. Every new field name creates a new field in the mapping, which lives in the cluster state, is broadcast to every node, and is capped by cluster.max_shards_per_node-adjacent limits (total_fields.limit, default 1000). Symptoms: slow cluster-state updates, nodes flapping, and eventually rejected writes. Fixes: flattened (one field holding the whole object, indexable but not individually sortable), object vs nested (object flattens and loses per-element association; nested keeps it, at the cost of a separate Lucene document per element and slower queries — use nested only when you must query array elements independently), dynamic templates, or index-per-entity-type.

Aggregations: terms (with doc_count_error_upper_count for shard-size skew — always check the error bound before trusting a facet count, and use composite for paginating more than 10,000 buckets), range/date_histogram, filter, nested, top_hits (a sub-search per bucket, powerful and slow), percentiles (TDigest, approximate), and cardinality (HyperLogLog++, approximate). Every aggregation scans matching docs, so aggregations over high-cardinality keyword fields are a memory risk (search.max_buckets, shard_size).

Deep pagination. from + size is capped at index.max_result_window (10,000) because every skipped result is materialized. Beyond that: search_after with a sort tuple, always combined with a pit (point in time) so the index cannot change under you mid-pagination. pit + search_after + a stable sort is the correct "keep scrolling" recipe, and it is also the right answer for polling an index that is being written to continuously.
Sorting. Always sort on a doc_values-backed field with a unique tiebreaker (_shard_doc when using a PIT, or a monotonic field). A non-deterministic sort produces duplicates and gaps between pages.

Index lifecycle management (ILM) / ISM. A phase model: hot (indexed, searchable), warm (replicated fewer, still searchable), cold (searchable with fewer resources or snapshot only), frozen (snapshot, no search), delete. Actions: rollover on size or age, shrink (merge shards to reduce shard count — do this after the index stops being written to), forcemerge (fewer, larger segments, faster search, expensive, read-only-ish), read_only, downsample (roll up metrics), and delete. A time-based index (logs-2026.01.15) plus max_age: 1d is the simplest correct retention story and it beats deleteByQuery, which is a full scan.

Search-as-you-type: the search_as_you_type field type provides title, title._2gram, title._3gram subfields plus bool_prefix and most_fields query types, so as the user types you get prefix matching with correct phrase-like behaviour. The alternative is a separate edge_ngram field. Both are better than prefix queries on keyword for latency, because edge_ngram is a term lookup in the inverted index while a prefix query must walk the term dictionary.

topics.title: OLTP vs OLAP, star schemas, and the pipelines
topics.description: OLTP vs OLAP, star schemas, and the pipelines within Database Systems: Additional Topics 25.
keyConcepts: Star schema rules

One fact table at the centre, with the grain stated in one sentence ("one row per order line per day"). If you cannot state the grain, you cannot aggregate correctly, and every analyst will aggregate differently.
Dimensions around it (product, customer, date, store), joined by surrogate integer keys. Conformed dimensions shared across facts are what make cross-domain reporting possible.

Slowly changing dimensions: type 1 overwrite (history lost, cheapest), type 2 add a new row with validity dates (correct history, needs valid_from/valid_to and a unique constraint ensuring no overlapping ranges), type 3 add a separate "previous value" column (rarely the right answer).

Snowflake normalizes dimensions into their own dimension tables to remove redundancy; it reduces storage and query fan-out costs but increases joins. Star denormalizes dimensions to speed up queries. Pick based on how often dimensions are queried independently.
Degenerate dimensions (a fact table with an order number but no order dimension) and factless fact tables (a row per attendance, per coverage) are real and worth naming.
Partitioning the fact table by date is the single most valuable physical decision: it enables partition pruning, makes retention a DROP PARTITION, and keeps the working set small.

Late-arriving facts and restatements are the hard part of analytics: a fact can change after you have computed aggregates over it. The standard answer is a defined "closed period" policy (today's numbers are provisional, and only closed periods are restated) plus an idempotent re-computation of the affected window. Do not try to make a mutable aggregate incremental over a mutable fact.
ETL vs ELT, and the three cadences

ETL transforms before loading (clean, dedupe, reshape in a compute layer, then load a small clean set). ELT loads raw first, then transforms in the warehouse, where SQL and storage are cheap. ELT has won almost everywhere because raw retention is valuable and the warehouse is the cheapest place to compute.

"Exactly once" is an illusion. Delivery is at-least-once almost everywhere, and end-to-end exactly-once requires a transactional sink, which most sinks are not. What you actually get is at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent sink: deduplicate by event id, or use a merge/upsert on a natural key, and make the sink write commutative. This is the answer to give when asked.

Late-arriving data is handled with event time, not processing time: use the timestamp inside the event for the window, maintain a watermark (the maximum event time seen minus an allowed lateness, advanced periodically), drop or route events older than the watermark to a late-arrival path, and recompute the affected closed windows. If you window on processing time, a five-minute-late event lands in the wrong bucket and your daily totals never reconcile.

topics.title: Object storage semantics
topics.description: Object storage semantics within Database Systems: Additional Topics 25.
keyConcepts: Multipart upload: CreateMultipartUpload → UploadPart (each part at least 5MB except the last, at most 10,000 parts, so the maximum object is about 5TB) → CompleteMultipartUpload. Benefits: resumable uploads of large files, parallel throughput, and per-part retry. Costs: you must clean up aborted uploads, and each part is a separate object until completion. Abandoned multipart uploads are billed forever — an AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle rule is the single most valuable line in an S3 lifecycle configuration.

ETag semantics: for a single-part upload the ETag is the MD5 of the content; for a multipart upload it is a hash of the part hashes, so it is not the MD5 and cannot be used for integrity verification. Use ChecksumAlgorithm (SHA-256) per part and per object if you need real verification, and verify on the download path.

Presigned URLs: a signed URL grants time-limited access to a specific key and method, which is how you upload directly from a browser without proxying bytes through your app. Critical details: the expiry (as short as possible, minutes for uploads), the Content-Type is part of the signature if you sign it, the URL is a bearer credential (anyone with it has access until expiry), and you must constrain the key prefix per user (PUT only under uploads/<userId>/) because a client that can choose any key can overwrite anything. Never sign a prefix wildcard.

Eventual consistency, carefully: PUT/GET of a single object is strongly read-after-write consistent in current S3. What is eventually consistent is: LIST (directory listings) and HEAD for an object that was just deleted or overwritten concurrently, CopyObject and DELETE interactions, and the replication to a secondary region (which is eventually consistent and is a documented design assumption). For strong consistency on listing behaviour, there is a consistent-read option in newer object stores; if you need a list-and-read invariant, design around it (a manifest object, or a database as the index).

No rename and no partial update. Renaming is CopyObject + Delete, which for a large object is a full server-side copy (billed) and is not atomic. Any "edit" of an object is a full new object. This is why object storage plus a pointer in a database is the pattern for "immutable objects, mutable references": the object is written once, and the row that points at it is updated in a transaction, and the old version is deleted later.

Versioning gives you rollback, and it interacts badly with cost: every delete becomes a marker, storage grows, and you must add lifecycle rules to expire non-current versions. Versioning is what makes accidental deletion recoverable, and it is worth enabling on anything you cannot regenerate.

Lifecycle rules are the cost control: expire by age, transition to infrequent-access or archive storage classes by age, abort incomplete multipart uploads after N days, and expire previous versions after N days. Archive storage classes have a *minimum* storage duration and a per-request retrieval fee, so a 30-day archive you read every day costs more than you think.

Range requests let you read a byte range, which is how you do partial downloads, parallel multi-part downloads of one object, and efficient range scans over a Parquet or NDJSON dataset. Every serious analytics pipeline on object storage exploits this.

Replication is asynchronous and eventually consistent. Cross-region replication adds latency to the secondary, and a read from the secondary immediately after a write can miss it. Design for that, or accept a single region.

The rule of thumb: object storage is for bytes, not for rows. It has no index, no transaction, no partial update, and no cheap random write. It is excellent for the source of truth for large immutable files, cheap archival, and lakehouse landing zones, and it is the wrong place for a mutable 200-byte record.
commonMistakes: assuming a write is instantly searchable; from-based deep pagination; sorting on _score alone with a paginated request; aggregations on a text field; keyword without ignore_above thought; synonyms in a production index with no reindex plan; a non-deterministic sort; using must for filters; expecting COUNT(*) from a terms agg to be exact on a large index; claiming exactly-once; windowing on processing time; leaving incomplete multipart uploads alive forever; trusting a multipart ETag as an MD5; a presigned URL that lets the client choose the key.
practiceTasks: index 500k products with a deliberately dirty feed (missing fields, a field that is sometimes a number and sometimes a string, a field that is sometimes null) and watch dynamic mapping guess wrong; then set dynamic: strict and add templates, and index again. Build a query with a phrase filter, a filter-clause tenant predicate, a facet, and a function_score decay, and measure the difference between filters in must and in filter. Then implement search_after with a PIT and prove that pagination is stable while you keep indexing new documents. Finally, put a flattened field, a nested array of objects, and a keyword field in one mapping and write a query for each.

topics.title: Social network: graph, feed, and fan-out
topics.description: Social network: graph, feed, and fan-out within Database Systems: Additional Topics 26.
keyConcepts: Follow/unfollow (directed), profiles, posts (text + media refs), reactions, comments (one level of nesting for v1).
Two feed products: a global "for you" feed and a following feed. Read-heavy (100k reads/s), write-light.
Feed freshness: seconds are acceptable. A reaction count that is 5 seconds stale is acceptable. A lost follow is not.
Privacy: a private account's posts are visible only to approved followers.
Entities and keys
Relationships and cardinality

User M:N User via follows (a directed, self-referencing adjacency list — the "join table that is a graph edge", see 6.22). PK on (follower_id, followee_id) gives the forward query; a separate index on followee_id gives the reverse ("who follows me") and is mandatory.

Post 1:N Comment; Post M:N User via reactions with the reaction kind as a non-key attribute (a PK on (post_id, user_id) means a user cannot switch from a like to a dislike; if that is required, PK on (post_id, user_id, kind) and accept duplicates, or make the key (post_id, user_id) and update the kind).
User 1:N Post, User 1:N Comment.
Normalization notes
3NF except the two count columns and the feed tables below.
follows must not be given a surrogate id; the composite PK *is* the identity, and it makes the follow an naturally idempotent.
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
users(id PK, handle UNIQUE, display_name, avatar_url, is_private, follower_count BIGINT, following_count BIGINT, created_at)
follows(follower_id FK, followee_id FK, created_at, PK(follower_id, followee_id))
posts(id PK, author_id FK, body, visibility, media jsonb, created_at, deleted_at)
reactions(post_id FK, user_id FK, kind, created_at, PK(post_id, user_id))    -- one reaction per user per post
comments(id PK, post_id FK, author_id FK, body, created_at, deleted_at)
post_counts(post_id PK, reactions BIGINT, comments BIGINT)                  -- denormalized
```

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON follows (followee_id, follower_id);       -- reverse direction
CREATE INDEX ON posts (author_id, created_at DESC) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
CREATE INDEX ON posts (created_at DESC) WHERE visibility = 'public' AND deleted_at IS NULL;
CREATE INDEX ON comments (post_id, created_at);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (lower(handle));             -- case-insensitive handle uniqueness
```

```sql
-- AP1: my following feed, keyset paged
SELECT p.id, p.author_id, p.body, p.created_at
FROM posts p
JOIN follows f ON f.follower_id = $1 AND f.followee_id = p.author_id
WHERE p.deleted_at IS NULL
  AND (p.created_at, p.id) < ($2, $3)
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC, p.id DESC
LIMIT 30;
-- This is the NESTED LOOP you must watch: with 500 follows it reads 500 index
-- ranges and sorts. It is fine at 500 and terrible at 50,000. The fan-out
-- materialisation below exists precisely because of this query.

-- AP2: who follows me (reverse), with count
SELECT count(*) FROM follows WHERE followee_id = $1;
SELECT u.id, u.handle, u.display_name, f.created_at
FROM follows f JOIN users u ON u.id = f.follower_id
WHERE f.followee_id = $1 ORDER BY f.created_at DESC LIMIT 50;

-- AP3: post detail with reaction count from the denormalized table
SELECT p.id, p.body, p.author_id, u.handle, pc.reactions, pc.comments
FROM posts p
JOIN users u ON u.id = p.author_id
LEFT JOIN post_counts pc ON pc.post_id = p.id
WHERE p.id = $1;

-- AP4: recommended users (people followed by people I follow, minus people I already follow)
WITH mine AS (SELECT followee_id FROM follows WHERE follower_id = $1),
     theirs AS (SELECT DISTINCT f.followee_id
                FROM follows f JOIN mine ON mine.followee_id = f.follower_id
                WHERE f.followee_id <> $1)
SELECT u.id, count(*) AS mutuals
FROM theirs JOIN users u ON u.id = theirs.followee_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM follows WHERE follower_id = $1 AND followee_id = theirs.followee_id)
GROUP BY u.id ORDER BY mutuals DESC LIMIT 20;
```

```js
// Bounded-depth follow-of-follow discovery on the edge collection, then rank.
db.follows.aggregate([
  { $match: { followerId: { $in: ['u1','u2','u3'] } } },     // people I follow (chunked)
  { $group: { _id: '$followeeId', mutuals: { $sum: 1 } } },   // collapse to candidates
  { $match: { _id: { $nin: ['u1','u2','u3'] } } },
  { $lookup: {                                                   // hydrate profiles
      from: 'users',
      localField: '_id', foreignField: '_id', as: 'profile'
  } },
  { $unwind: '$profile' },
  { $addFields: {
      score: { $add: [
        { $multiply: ['$mutuals', 10] },
        { $ln: { $add: [1, { $ifNull: ['$profile.followerCount', 0] } } } }
      ] }
  } },
  { $sort: { score: -1 } },
  { $limit: 20 },
  { $project: { _id: 1, score: 1,
                handle: '$profile.handle', displayName: '$profile.displayName' } }
], { allowDiskUse: true, maxTimeMS: 300 });
```

Database sequence per conversation (seq from a counter service or from a SERIAL on a per-conversation table). Ordering is authoritative, gapless, and you can page with seq < cursor. Cost: an extra round trip or a contended counter on the hot path.

Client-generated sortable ids (UUIDv7 or a Snowflake-style id with timestamp + conversation + counter). Ordering is derived from the id, no round trip, and ids are unique across clients. Cost: ids from different senders can be slightly out of order (clock skew), and there can be gaps.

topics.title: In-memory cache with LRU + TTL + single-flight
topics.description: In-memory cache with LRU + TTL + single-flight within Database Systems: Additional Topics 27.
keyConcepts: Edge cases and what a strong answer says about each

Undefined values. peek returning undefined conflates "absent" with "cached undefined". Either forbid undefined values or return a sentinel/{ hit: boolean } wrapper. The production version caches a NULL sentinel for negative caching.

Clock injection. The #now parameter exists so tests can advance time deterministically; a real implementation also protects against a system clock that jumps backwards, which would make entries live longer than intended. Date.now() is wall-clock and not monotonic; a monotonic clock is correct for TTLs.

LRU vs LFU vs TTL interaction. A key that is constantly read but has a 5s TTL is evicted by TTL, not by LRU, so the LRU order only matters for keys that have not expired. If you sweep lazily on access, expired entries still consume memory — hence sweep() on a timer.

Single-flight leaks. The finally must delete the in-flight entry, or a failed loader poisons the key forever. Also, a loader that never resolves leaks the entry forever, so a loader timeout is mandatory in production.

Unbounded loaders. If one key is requested a million times while loading, a million callers await one promise; that is correct but the promise's resolution is a thundering herd of continuations. Cap the waiter count or shed load above a threshold.
Stampede across processes. This only fixes the single-process case. The distributed versions are a lock, early recompute, or stale-while-revalidate (6.27.6).
Not thread-safe in a worker-thread sense; if you need that, wrap the map in a mutex or use one cache per thread (which loses the shared hit rate).

Eviction of a hot key is the failure everyone misses: a key at exactly the capacity boundary can be evicted and immediately reloaded by the next reader, in a loop. Early recompute plus a max headroom factor mitigates it.

topics.title: Minimal DataLoader with batching and per-request caching
topics.description: Minimal DataLoader with batching and per-request caching within Database Systems: Additional Topics 27.
keyConcepts: Edge cases
Order and length must match. The batch function must return exactly one result per input key, in the same order. Mismatch is the classic bug; the length assertion above is the guard.
Per-key errors: return an Error instance in the results array rather than rejecting the whole batch, so one missing row does not fail 200 requests. That is why the return type is V | Error.

Deduplication within a tick, not across ticks: two loads in the same microtask collapse to one key; two loads in different ticks do not, unless a cached promise exists (which it does, because the promise is cached from the moment of load). Real DataLoader keeps the cached promise, so cross-tick duplicates are also deduplicated — the #seen set only guards the *queue*.
A module-level loader caches forever. It must be created per request. This is the DataLoader data-leak bug and it is worth naming unprompted.

Batch function re-entrancy: if the batch function itself calls load on the same loader, you deadlock unless the flush is already scheduled. Real implementations document that you must not do this; a separate loader per level avoids it.
Max batch size exists to keep the IN (...) list under the parameter limit and the query planner happy.
Unbounded cache growth: a long-lived loader holds every key it ever saw. Per-request scope solves it; otherwise add a TTL or an LRU.

queueMicrotask vs process.nextTick vs setTimeout(0): the dispatch must happen after the current synchronous block, so the caller can enqueue several loads. queueMicrotask is the tightest and the conventional choice.

topics.title: Cache-aside helper with stale-while-revalidate and stampede protection
topics.description: Cache-aside helper with stale-while-revalidate and stampede protection within Database Systems: Additional Topics 27.
keyConcepts: The state machine, which is the actual content of this exercise

The three TTLs, not two. softTtl (freshness), hardTtl (staleness ceiling), and the refresh timeout. Setting only one TTL means either serving stale data forever after a failed refresh (bad) or never being fresh (pointless).

Single-flight is the stampede protection, and it is what makes the STALE path safe: 1,000 concurrent readers of a stale key trigger one load, and the other 999 get the stale value *immediately* rather than waiting. That is the whole point of SWR: the request is never blocked after the first fill.

The #inflight map is separate from entry.refreshing on purpose. #inflight guards *all* concurrent loads including hard misses; entry.refreshing guards the *background* refresh so a stale key does not spawn a refresh per reader. Confusing the two is the most common bug in hand-rolled SWR.
A failed refresh must not delete the entry. Serving slightly-stale data beats serving a 500. That is the onErrorServeStale behaviour, and a circuit breaker around load is the production addition.

Early recompute (refresh inside the last 20% of the stale window) removes the synchronized-expiry wave that plain TTL creates. Combined with #ttlJitter, it is the difference between a smooth miss rate and a periodic cliff.
Negative caching needs a sentinel value, not null, or null results are reloaded forever.

The distributed version replaces #inflight with a Redis lock plus a short sleep-and-retry, and the state must live in Redis (or the entry is per-process and the SWR benefit disappears across a fleet).
